en: Preface to the Commentary on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, composed by Chu Liang, Great Director of the Academy (Dachang Boshi) of Henan:

Now, as for the Great Mass [of Nature] which equalizes all forms, beings employ their intelligence and follow external objects; their dispositions change according to habituation, and their thoughts shift with circumstances. Thus it is that...
His penetrating discernment and exhaustive vision were as clear as those of a sage who has attained prior awakening;
he held aloft the brilliant torch of wisdom to emerge from the profound darkness and pulled himself from the river of craving to ascend to the further shore.

This cannot be discussed in the same breath as those who have transmigrated through ten thousand kalpas, stained by the six sense-objects, drifting aimlessly in pursuit of the infinite, or galloping headlong toward the shortcut of worldly existence. Yingchuan Yu Chusun, from his youth, widely propagated sincere faith.
Illuminated by Prajñā, he returned to the Right Path; manifesting the names and characteristics of the Mahāyāna, he established the ultimate tenet of non-abiding.
Transcending the realm of thought and surging beyond the bounds of words and images, he bound his hair in a topknot and received the precepts many years ago.

Although his recitation has never faltered despite the eloquent expositions of the Dharma, the profound and deep source of spiritual power may still contain that which has not yet been fully realized.
I lament that those who have lost their way do not realize they are not far from it; looking toward the broad, level path, I heave a great sigh of relief.

At this time, there is the Dharma Master Huìjìng, whose profound mastery of the abstruse meanings is as versatile as a heated girdle and whose investigation of principles is as seamless as a linked chain. Having entered the inner chamber of Master Yǔ and studied its subtle nuances, I have humbly accepted his excellent guidance.

Building upon this vow, I further requested him to provide a commentary. The Dharma Master held up the mirror of wisdom without weariness, while I remained like one squatting in a crossroads, full of self-satisfaction.
Relying on the Way of divine response, he exhausts the functions of the human mind; he expounds the subtle words and proclaims the ultimate principles.
Former doubts are dissolved like ice melting in water, and the wondrous meanings of today shine brightly as dawn breaks through the clouds.

He serves as the beam and pillar for the Semblance Dharma, transforming the ears and eyes of all living beings. The peaks of his eloquence are exquisite, surpassing Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in loftiness; the springs of his speech gush forth with vigor.

In his prime, he journeyed to the Dragon Palace to vie with those who travel afar. Now, as the teachings of Śākyamuni arose in the West and the source of the Way flowed eastward, generations have passed;

though men of wisdom and talent have appeared, few have possessed such comprehensive mastery and profound insight into the sublime intent. Today, the śramaṇa has once again expounded these teachings, bringing them to great renown in this age.
I imagine that this Esoteric School will become preeminent. In the month of Jia-mao, at the beginning of the year, I first took it up in my breast-pocket.

In the month of Zhōnglǜ, I here bring this pen to rest. Monastics and laypeople alike look up to him; the canopies of their carriages form a dense shade. As bells are struck according to their size, they ring out;
as swords are drawn, they flash with brilliance. His contemporaries, fellow students who specialized in his teachings, all entered these profound waves of wisdom and transmitted them one to another.
Yet he alone looked down upon Lín Yuǎn and An Shēng with indifference, walking solitary on the high road to proclaim the True Dharma.
The Dharma of Liaodong is a true original that rivals the "Hanging Gold" for its rarity;
as the destination of the "Guiding South," it treasures the "Clustered Jade" so that it shall never decay. How magnificent! How magnificent!
The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Volume One,
with Commentary by Śramaṇa Huìjìng of Jìguó Monastery.
Thus it was said.
"Xin" (faith/conviction) refers to words. When there is faith, the principles of what is spoken accord with reality; when they accord, the way of teacher and disciple is perfected.
Words need not be either prolix or concise; yet without faith, they cannot be transmitted. Therefore, the established teaching is as follows.

"I heard" (I-wen) refers to verified hearing. To say "I heard" in person means to have received it directly from the source; to say "that which was heard" implies having received it through transmission.
This instance of "I heard" indicates that the words were personally received from the Master’s lips.
At one time,
it was an auspicious day— the day the Dharma King inaugurated his reign, a time of great assembly for the multitude.
The Buddha—

He is the Master of Transformation. The name of the Great Teacher takes "awakening" (bodhi) as its essential meaning: first, self-awakening; second, awakening others; and third, the fulfillment of awakening.

He is distinguished from ordinary people by his self-awakening; he is distinguished from those of the Two Vehicles by his awakening of others; and he is distinguished from bodhisattvas by the fulfillment of his awakening.
When these three conditions were fulfilled, he received the name of Buddha.
He was at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park;
this was his place of transformation. The kingdom was the sphere of his travels, and the park was his place of residence. He dwelt in the kingdom for the sake of transforming beings.
Those who remain in the secular world reside in the gardens as leaders of the monastic community.

Śrāvastī is translated here as "Country of Heard Objects" (聞物國), for excellent things are produced in this land and its fine reputation resounds far across all nations; thus it is called the Country of Heard Objects.
Jeta was the name of the crown prince; this is translated as "Victorious in Battle. At the time of the prince's birth, the King defeated his enemies.
The army’s rebel was reported to the throne by an official, who then provided his name. "Givaka" (Gee-tan) is a title for a state minister; his original name was Sudatta.
Sudatta was compassionate within and wealthy without, providing relief to the poor and succoring the widowed.
The people of the district praised him, and thus he was given this title. The garden was purchased by Sudatta, while the trees were donated by Jeta; the trees were a separate offering.
"Ārāma" (Garden) is the general name. Since the sovereign is superior and the subject is subordinate, one cannot simply call it "the Garden of Jeta.

Since the garden is the whole and the trees are its parts, one cannot merely say "the Trees of Jeta. Therefore, both are used together. As for the separate acts of purchasing the garden and donating the trees, these matters are distinct.
He was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus;
they all heard [the teaching] together. There are three meanings of "bhikṣu": first, "one who terrifies Māra"; second, "a mendicant"; and third, "one who destroys evil.
Terrifying Māra comes first; the mendicant follows next; and destroying evil is last. Now, when one first establishes the path of the profound gate...
Having resolved to subdue Māra, he thus shaved his hair and donned the dyed robes; the celestial palaces trembled and Māra was struck with fear.
As the body serves as the vessel for the Way, when the body is at peace, the Way flourishes; therefore, once he has been moistened by the Dharma-robes, he must beg for food to sustain his body.
The path of the noble ones lengthens, while the path of ordinary beings diminishes; therefore, when one's cultivation is complete, one immediately destroys evil to realize the fruit.
At that time, the World-Honored One—

The preceding section clarifies the general introduction (sūtra-opening) to provide verification; the following section clarifies the specific introduction to initiate [the discourse]. It establishes the World-Honored One as the Teacher who transforms beings.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states that because he possesses the nine aforementioned titles, he is called the "World-Honored One" (Bhagavat).
The time for eating (*bhojana-kāla*) is the hour of the *Chen* (辰) constellation. At dawn, the preparation of the meal begins; by late afternoon, the eating of the meal is finished.

There is no [other] time like that between the hours of *Mo* (末, 10–11 AM) and *Wu* (午, 11 AM–1 PM), which is precisely the period when the meal is first ready. Since one goes on alms-round during this hour, it is called "the time for eating."

Wearing robes and carrying an alms bowl are the manifestations of his transformative conduct (*nirmāṇa*). He wears robes because some non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) do not wear them; he carries an alms bowl because some hold their food in their hands.
Thus, he wears robes to refute the naked ascetics (*nirgrantha*), and he carries an alms bowl to refute those who eat from their hands. He is clad in the monastic robes.
Wearing the kāṣāya robe, he is thus said to be "clad in robes. Holding the alms bowl offered by the Four Heavenly Kings, he is thus said to be "carrying the bowl.
He entered the great city of Śrāvastī, which is the place of his transformation.
This city has nine hundred million households and measures twelve yojanas in length and breadth; therefore, it is called "great. [The park...]
The south is the city wall and the north is the interior; proceeding from the outside toward the inside is therefore called "entering.
Begging for food is an act of transformation. By following this [path] to beg for food, one becomes a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) for others.
Within that city, having completed his sequential alms-round, he transformed [himself] into an equal [of the poor].
Now, to abandon the wealthy and follow the poor benefits the poor but does not benefit the wealthy;

to abandon the poor and follow the wealthy benefits the wealthy but does not benefit the poor. It was for this reason that Mahākāśyapa was rebuked for abandoning the wealthy to follow the poor. Abandoning the poor...
Because [the Buddha] was wealthy, Subhūti set aside his bowl; now the Buddha does not do so, and thus it is said that he "begs in sequence.
He then returns to his original place.
He is content. Because of contentment, he begs no more than is necessary. Because of delighting in solitude, he returns to his original dwelling.
Having finished his meal, [he departs].

This concludes the section on transformation. Since the body of a Vajra-being does not depend upon food for sustenance, it manifests the appearance of eating rice solely for the purpose of benefiting sentient beings.
Having described the practice of wandering for alms above, the following clarifies the arrangement of the seat and entry into stillness, intended to cause sentient beings to generate merit.
Therefore, he goes forth on the road to beg for alms in order to cause sentient beings to give rise to wisdom. Therefore, he enters seclusion before preaching;
the gathering of robes and bowl serves to eliminate external conditions. He puts on the saṃghāṭī robe for the purpose of entering a village.
Having accepted the alms bowls of the Four Heavenly Kings to store provisions for the journey, he returned to his original location. His old robes must be put away;
once the meal is finished, his old bowl must be set aside.
Having washed his feet, he applied ointment to remove the impurities from them; through reverent concentration, he purified his person.
He spread out a seat and sat down.

This is the proper entry into stillness. As he was about to preach the Dharma, he spread out the lion seat; as he was about to enter meditative concentration, it was appropriate for him to sit in the full lotus posture.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti:
the preceding section clarifies the introduction, explaining the origins of the undertaking; the following section clarifies the essence of the sūtra, manifesting the benefits realized while seated.
"Elder" (*sthavira*) is a term of honor. "Subhūti" is translated here as "Śubhamati" (Good Fortune) or "Gaganagañja" (Born of Emptiness); at the time of his birth, his chamber...

Exhausting all emptiness, he is therefore called "Born of Emptiness" (Kōshō). When his parents questioned him, the Master said, "Only good, only auspicious," and thus he was named "Good Auspiciousness" (Zenki).
From within the great assembly, he immediately rose from his seat.
However, one who honors others and values the Dharma cannot, by principle, remain seated with hands folded; how much less so when being requested for instruction on a specific matter?
Therefore, he shifts his body to avoid his seat and bares his right shoulder.
This both expresses the etiquette between teacher and disciple and demonstrates the appearance of being exhorted and guided; it also accords with the laws of the state,
whereby one shows reverence by baring the right shoulder and placing the right knee upon the ground.
They bowed down in submission, showing no appearance of resistance or refusal;
with palms joined in reverence,
they composed their countenances in solemnity, manifesting a mind of single-minded devotion.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying: "How rare, World-Honored One!
Since you wish to request the Way, it is fitting that you first extol its virtues. The intent behind extolling virtues serves as the very foundation for requesting further instruction.
These words, 'How rare, World-Honored One,' constitute a general eulogy to introduce the chapter."

*Tathāgata* means "thus" (*tathā*), referring to *tathatā* (suchness); "come" (*āgata*) refers to non-discriminative wisdom (*avikalpa-jñāna*). "Thus" takes non-differentiation as its meaning; "come" takes reaching the destination as its function.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time have all come by means of non-discriminative wisdom, riding upon the path of *tathatā*.
Having attained perfect enlightenment, he is therefore called the Tathāgata.
He skillfully protects and mindfully cares for all bodhisattvas, and skillfully entrusts them to all bodhisattvas.

"Bodhisattva" is here translated as "sentient beings with the aspiration for the Way. His protective mindfulness pertains to the time of turning the wheel of Dharma, when he transforms those who practice deeply.

Regarding the Bodhisattva’s entrustment at the time of *parinirvāṇa*: "Protecting" refers to protecting and guarding oneself through the power of wisdom, thereby causing the Buddha-dharma to be accomplished.
"Mindfulness" refers to taking one's transformed disciples as the object [of attention] through the power of teaching, thereby causing sentient beings to be accomplished.
There are three powers of transformation: first, the wheel of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-cakra*).

Second is the wheel of reading minds; third is the wheel of the correct teaching. Through the transformation of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), one is able to cause those who turn their backs on the heterodox to return to the orthodox.

Through the reality of reading minds and speech, one is able to cause the removal of doubt and the arising of faith. Through the correct teaching that reveals principle, one is able to cause the abandonment of evil and the cultivation of goodness.
Regarding "entrustment" (*parindanā*): "entrust" (*pu*) means to take what is shallow and confer it upon the profound; "belonging" (*shu*) refers to instruction.

The profound transforms the shallow. Regarding the two types of merit for a bodhisattva of shallow practice—namely, that which has already been attained and that which has not yet been attained—the purpose is to ensure that what has been attained is not lost, and to cause what has not yet been attained to increase through cultivation.
Therefore, the shallow is entrusted to the profound, so that the profound may transform them and prevent them from falling back.

"World-Honored One, when it is said that they are 'good men and good women,' this distinguishes them from the class of icchantikas and non-Buddhists. When it is said 'men and women,' this excludes those with dual sexual organs or eunuchs."
One generates the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
*An* means "non-"; *uttara* means "supreme"; *sam* means "correct"; *yak* means "pervasive"; the latter three [syllables] mean "knowledge"; *bodhi* means "awakening.

Taken together, it is called "Unsurpassed Correct Pervasive Knowledge-Awakening. "Correct" refers to the wisdom that accords with reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*); "pervasive" refers to the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*).
*Jñāna-pramāṇa* (measuring wisdom) refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). *Bodha* (awakening) refers to the subsequent wisdom following non-conceptual wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

Because wisdom according to principle (*yathāvad-jñāna*) takes the ultimate truth as its object, it is called "correct" (*samyak*). Because wisdom according to phenomena (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) takes the conventional truth as its object, it is called "pervasive" (*vyāpin*).

Because non-conceptual wisdom eliminates the two kinds of ignorance (*ajñāna*), it is called "knowing" (*jñāna*). Because the subsequent wisdom following non-conceptual wisdom transcends the state of sleep and dreams, it is called "awakening" (*bodha*). This...
The four wisdoms constitute the very essence of the Buddha-fruit. If a person resolves their mind to seek this essence from afar, it is called "generating the bodhicitta.
This is established as the basis for the inquiry.
"How should one dwell? How should one subdue the mind?
Now, although the Dharma gates are vast, they do not exceed the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna, nor the causal virtue and the resultant virtue.
This sutra reveals the gateways of the Mahāyāna and clarifies the correct practice of bodhisattvas. For this reason, it requests [an explanation of] the cause rather than the fruit;
for since the fruit is necessarily attained through the cause, it also cites the fruit merely to clarify the cause.

There are three types of causes clarified in the Mahāyāna: first, the cause that ought to be attained; second, the cause of application; and third, the cause of perfection. That which ought to be attained refers to...
The bodhicitta. That which is to be practiced refers to the conduct of the ten perfections (daśapāramitā). That which is to be fulfilled refers to the fruit of the three virtues (triguṇa-phala).

The arousal of the mind (cittotpāda) is caused by the buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha); the initiation of practice is caused by the arousal of the mind; and the perfecting of the fruit is caused by applied cultivation (prayoga).
Therefore, the buddha-nature is taken as the cause for that which is to be attained, the arousal of the mind as the cause for applied cultivation, and applied cultivation as the cause for perfection.
This is the cause for fulfillment. This passage should contain three questions. The first asks, "How does one abide? This requests the cause of the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
It says, "One desires to generate the bodhicitta"; it asks by abiding in what state of mind one accomplishes its generation. The second question asks, "How does one practice?"
This is the request for the complete cause [of practice]. It states: "I wish to cultivate the bodhisattva conduct. What kind of conduct must be initiated to accomplish this cultivation?
The subsequent question asks: "How does one subdue the mind? This is the request for the secondary complete cause. It states: "I wish to eliminate the obstacles to correct practice.
What kind of mind must be subdued to accomplish this elimination? Now, since there are three causes, why are only the latter two requested? As for the first cause...

There is that which exists from the beginning (*pūrvabhava*). That which exists from the beginning is not the work of the Buddha (*buddhakārya*). The latter two are newly arisen (*navotpāda*). That which is newly arisen is the work of the Buddha.
Regarding that which is not the work of the Buddha: it exists even when there is no teaching, and it exists even when there is teaching.

For this reason, it is established spontaneously without depending on inquiry. Regarding that which is the work of the Buddha: it exists when there is teaching, and it does not exist when there is no teaching. For this reason, it is necessarily...
It was established because of this request.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is as you have said: the Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas;
he well entrusts all bodhisattvas."
I praise [this teaching] before I explain it, for I hold its words in high esteem.
Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you. Son of good family, daughter of good family:
having resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, you should abide in this manner and subdue your mind in this manner.
He cautioned him before granting permission, thereby focusing his intention.
"So be it, World-Honored One; I wish most earnestly to hear [your teaching].
Having received permission, the Elder spoke of his aspiration out of compassion.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this manner. The term *mahā* means "great"; thus, they are great bodhisattvas.
To answer the first question, he speaks of "subduing" because it means causing them to abide in the fourfold grace (*caturvidha-anugraha*) when they resolve their minds [on awakening];
this is precisely what subdues the minds of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles. The fourfold grace:

These are: first, the expansive mind; second, the supreme mind; third, the constant mind; and fourth, the non-erroneous mind. The first two clarify that one can be pervasive through the perfection [of wisdom]; this is to use the expansive to subdue the narrow.
The latter two clarify that there is nothing to be perfected through the perfection [of wisdom]; this is to use the non-existent to subdue the existent.
Using the expansive to subdue the narrow is to subdue the minds of those of the Two Vehicles. Using the non-existent to subdue the existent is to subdue the minds of ordinary worldlings.
Subduing the minds of ordinary beings manifests the possession of wisdom; subduing the minds of those of the Two Vehicles clarifies the possession of compassion.
This is the general instruction first; what follows is the specific exposition.
"All sentient beings of every kind.

This clarifies the breadth of his grace. Regarding the categories of sentient beings, three are now briefly cited; these are presented first as a general enumeration before the specific classes are listed.
Whether born from an egg, born from a womb, born from moisture, or born by transformation—these enumerate the classes of birth.

"Birth" refers to the new arising of the sense faculties (*indriya*). That which is produced from an egg is called "egg-born"; that which emerges from being contained within [the mother] is called "womb-born";
that which arises through reliance on moisture is called "moisture-born"; and that which appears suddenly is called "transformation-born."
Whether with form (*rūpin*) or without form (*arūpin*), these are the categories of the realms (*dhātu*).
"Realm" (*dhātu*) has the meaning of differentiation. First, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); second, the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); third, the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The desire realm necessarily includes that which has form; the form realm is necessarily devoid of desire; in the single formless realm, there is no form.
"Without desire. To say "if there is form" refers to encompassing the sentient beings of the two lower realms;
to say "if there is no form" refers to encompassing the sentient beings of the upper realm.
Whether there is perception, or non-perception, or neither-perception-nor-non-perception—these enumerate the categories of nature.
"Nature" (prakṛti) means essence (svabhāva). All sentient beings take perception as their nature.

First, those with perception: this refers to having a mind that is coarse. Second, those without perception: this refers to being without a mind and quiescent. Third, those who have neither perception nor... [non-perception].
"Neither-perception" (*asaṃjñin*) means that although there is mind, it is neither coarse nor quiescent. Because it is not coarse, it differs from "having perception" (*saṃjñin*);

because it is not quiescent, it differs from "non-perception" (*asaṃjñika*). Therefore, it is called "neither having perception," and so forth. If one says "having perception," this includes the seven meditative attainments of having perception as well as sentient beings of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
If one says "non-perception," this includes the two types of non-perceptual attainments (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and...

These are the sentient beings of the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*). When it says "neither with perception nor without perception," this includes the sentient beings of the Heaven of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
These are all objects of the expansive mind; those who seek the unsurpassed path should first abide in these states and then resolve their minds [upon enlightenment].
"I shall cause all to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and bring them to final liberation.
This clarifies the first kind of grace. Although there have been extensive deliverances previously, if one bestows the bliss of humans and devas, it is called "inferior grace.
If one bestows the bliss of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), it is called "middling grace. If one bestows the bliss of Great *Nirvāṇa*, it is called [the supreme grace].
The Supreme Benevolence. *Nirvāṇa* takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its essence and "quiescent cessation" as its meaning. "Quiescence" refers to the stilling of the causes of the three delusions;
"cessation" refers to the ending of the retributions of the three sufferings. Because it quiets the causes of delusion, the designation "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*) is established;

because it ceases the retribution of suffering, the term "without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*) is established. "I cause all to enter" expresses the mind capable of bestowing this grace. This is "without remainder."
Nirvana is the essence of the bestowed grace; to bring about extinction (parinirvāṇa) is the primary act of bestowing that grace.
Thus, although he brings immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings to extinction, in reality, there is no sentient being who attains extinction.
This clarifies constant grace. The reason a bodhisattva is able to transform beings constantly is that they cultivate both compassion and wisdom together.
If one has compassion but lacks wisdom, one becomes mired in existence and gives rise to weariness.

If one has wisdom but lacks compassion, one clings to emptiness and seeks realization. If one practices wisdom while maintaining compassion, one contemplates emptiness without grasping. If one maintains...

One practices compassion while possessing wisdom; thus, one transforms beings constantly and without ceasing. To say that "in this way, immeasurable sentient beings are brought to extinction" clarifies that there is compassion in transforming the mundane world.
To say that "in reality, no sentient being attains extinction" reveals that there is wisdom regarding the ultimate truth.
Because there is wisdom regarding the ultimate truth, self and others are of one essence; because there is compassion in transforming the mundane world, one acts constantly and without ceasing.

Why is this? The following clarifies the non-perverted nature of their kindness. A doubt is raised: "The preceding passage speaks of 'extinguishing sentient beings,' while the subsequent passage speaks of 'attaining extinction through non-arising. What does this mean?"
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span, they are not a bodhisattva.
These four attachments of "self" and so forth are the mind of conceptual discrimination; the mind of conceptual discrimination is the primary obstacle for a bodhisattva. There is...
If we possess the notion of a self, our own delusions have not yet been extinguished; such persons are not Bodhisattvas. Possessing such inversions, how could they transform sentient beings?
Conversely, those who are free from the notion of a self have exhausted their own delusions and are thus called Bodhisattvas.
Because they are free from inversion, they are able to constantly transform others.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving without dwelling on any phenomenon. From this point forward, the answer to the question regarding cultivation is given;
"practice" here refers specifically to giving. Now, giving is taught in order to bring about freedom from the three obstacles.

First is the obstacle of non-practice; second is the obstacle of deviant practice; third is the obstacle of inverted practice. Not being attached to one's own person removes the obstacle of non-practice;
not being attached to gratitude removes the obstacle of deviant practice; not being attached to karmic retribution removes the obstacle of inverted practice.
Now, as for being attached to one's own person: one loves oneself and hates others, possesses stinginess and lacks generosity; and lacking generosity is precisely non-practice.

This refers to the obstacle of practicing [with attachment to] phenomena (*dharma*). This passage is missing from the current edition. An alternative version states: "One practices giving without dwelling upon things. "Things" refers here to one's own person.

"One should have no dwelling-place with respect to phenomena" means that this removes the obstacle of deviant practice regarding phenomena. As for "phenomena": *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)*

This refers to the sphere of those who have shown kindness. It encompasses such acts as making offerings and showing respect, as well as praising their names and extolling their virtues; because these matters are numerous and extensive, they are summarized here by means of Dharma discourse. If one practices giving with the aim of seeking such a reward, it is called "deviant conduct. As for "deviant": *The Sutra on the Deviant Path* states: "If one gives with the thought of seeking a reward, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking fame, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking reputation, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking praise, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking a good name, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking a high status, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking wealth, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking power, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking a beautiful appearance, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking a long life, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking a noble lineage, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking a large retinue, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking a great following, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking a great realm, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking a great kingdom, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking a great city, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking a great country, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking a great state, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking a great clan, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking a great family, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking a great house, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking a great residence, this is called deviant giving. If one gives with the thought of seeking a great palace, this is called deviant giving. Dust. This means that one immediately relinquishes the primary retribution (the physical body) and practices giving solely for the sake of unsurpassed bodhi; this is the correct practice of a Bodhisattva.

Next, the response to the question on subduing [the three spheres] is given: the "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) are that which is dwelt upon, and the "mind" (citta) is that which dwells. "Characteristics" refers to the substance of the three spheres:
first, the characteristic of the giver; second, the characteristic of the recipient; and third, the characteristic of the material gift. "Mind" refers to the conceptualization of the three spheres.

The notion of a giver, the notion of a recipient, and the notion of material wealth—these characteristics constitute the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which is the fetter of characteristics (*nimitta-bandhana*).
The notions themselves constitute the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which is the fetter of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya-bandhana*). These two are the primary obstacles for a bodhisattva.

If a bodhisattva practices the contemplation of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva-vipaśyanā*), they realize that conceptual construction is fundamentally without characteristics; thus, the fetter of characteristics is extinguished. Since the dependent nature is fundamentally without arising, [the fetter of coarse heaviness is likewise extinguished].

Therefore, the heavy burdens [of affliction] are extinguished. If one can practice each of the six perfections while remaining free from the three characteristics and the three perceptions, this is precisely the subduing of the mind that clings to signs and the accomplishment of signless conduct.
Why is this? One might ask:
"What harm is there in abiding in signs? What benefit is there in abandoning signs? Why must one abandon signs and not abide in them?
If a bodhisattva practices giving without abiding in signs, the resulting merit and virtue are inconceivable and immeasurable.
The answer is that merit is difficult to measure. Why? Because the signless is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), while the signful is the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
Ultimate truth is pervasive; conventional affairs are obstructive. A mind free of signs accords with ultimate truth without limit;
how, then, could the merit produced by it be measured by conventional affairs?
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the space of the eastern direction be measured?

What precedes is the correct answer according to the questions; from here on, the doubts are severed based on those answers. The "correct answer" consists of the brief exposition that establishes the fundamental tenet (*mūla-siddhānta*);

Regarding the elimination of doubt through correct practice, the doubt is as follows: "If practicing causes while dwelling upon signs can evoke a retribution with signs, then practicing causes while forgetting signs should result in a fruit without signs.
Why, then, did the World-Honored One originally practice the cause of forgetting signs?"
Now that there is a fruit with characteristics, it is clear that since the fruit possesses characteristics, the cause cannot be non-abiding.

Because the Buddha wished to sever this doubt, he posed a question to resolve it: "Can one perceive the wondrous essence within the ultimate reality by means of the physical marks of the provisional realm—namely, the thirty-two marks?"
"No, World-Honored One. One cannot see the Tathāgata by means of physical marks.
Subhūti accepted the blade and replied: "Physical marks are illusory, whereas the Tathāgata is the reality.
One cannot rely on the illusory to perceive the true essence."
Why is this? The bodily marks (*kāyalakṣaṇa*) spoken of by the Tathāgata are, in fact, not bodily marks.
To clarify this point: that bodily marks are not bodily marks involves, in brief, three meanings: first, by way of aggregation; second, by way of characteristics;
and third, by way of nature. Regarding aggregation: the bodily marks take the infinitesimal atom (*paramāṇu*) as their substance, consisting of nine or ten subtle particles.

Regarding the aggregate (*rāśi*): if one analyzes it according to its spatial divisions, it is necessarily exhausted upon reaching the level of the infinitesimal atom (*paramāṇu*). Regarding [analysis] by way of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*):
the characteristic of the body has conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as its substance, with the eight factors such as arising (*jāti*) as its characteristics;

if one investigates it according to its temporal sequence, it collapses of itself at the limit of a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). Regarding [analysis] by way of nature (*svabhāva*): the characteristic of the body has the objective sphere (*viṣaya*) as its substance, and it functions through discrimination (*vikalpa*).
Nature is nature; it is observed by way of signlessness (*animitta*). Upon entering consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), it becomes emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
By virtue of these three meanings, one must not observe the Tathāgata through signs.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All marks whatsoever are empty and false. If one perceives all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.
Subhūti replied in accordance with the Buddha's mind, and the Buddha further established its meaning: "All marks whatsoever are ordinary."
The eight characteristics, such as arising and so forth, are all false and illusory; they do not transcend the three natures, such as the aggregate (*skandha*) and the rest.

If one perceives that these various characteristics are non-characteristics, one dispels the illusory to enter the real, thereby seeing the Tathāgata. By realizing the real, one becomes detached from the illusory.
If this is so, then practicing causes while forgetting characteristics is a fruit obtained by relying upon *tathatā* (suchness); how could it have anything to do with having characteristics? No.
One may perceive the characteristics of skillful means and take those characteristics to be the truth; thus, one slanders the cause by means of the fruit and harbors doubt regarding the cause.

At that time, although there will be many who lack faith, there will still be those who believe and accept it.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "For monastics, ethical discipline (*śīla*) is the foremost; for lay bodhisattvas, generosity (*dāna*) is the foremost."
He is the foremost. Regarding these chapters and verses:

"chapter" (parivarta) refers to a major section. The preceding portion explains the profound cause of non-abiding; this constitutes one chapter. The subsequent portion explains signlessness (animitta).
This profound fruit forms another chapter. Its phrases and words are detailed and precise: it does not abide within causes, nor does it dwell within the flow of form and so forth;
it is the category wherein, within the fruit of signlessness, signs are themselves non-signs.
One is able to give rise to faith and take this as reality.
Faith is the cause for non-abiding practice; it will necessarily result in the fruit of formlessness. Therefore, it is said that one takes this as reality.
It should be known that this person has not planted roots of goodness under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas;
rather, they have already planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable thousands of millions of Buddhas.
There are three roots of goodness: first, non-avarice; second, non-hatred; and third, non-delusion.

By means of these roots of goodness, one burns incense and scatters flowers within the field of the Buddha, invoking his name and extolling his virtues; therefore, it is called "planting. This does not refer to a single Buddha alone.
The roots of their merit are not shallow; they have already planted blessings for immeasurable eons.
As for those who hear these words and passages and give rise to even a single thought of pure faith:
To show that although their faith may be slight, their merit is great, it is said: "even for a single thought-moment.
Subhūti, the Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees all these sentient beings.
Fleshly vision (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) is seeing but not knowing; inferential knowledge (*anumāna-jñāna*) is knowing but not seeing; realized knowledge (*sākṣāt-kriyā-jñāna*) is both seeing and knowing.

By saying "knowing," it clarifies that this is not what is seen by fleshly vision; by saying "seeing," it clarifies that this is not what is known by inferential knowledge—it is precisely realized knowledge.
It knows their names and bodies and sees their forms and activities; therefore, the two terms are used together.

To "attain such immeasurable merit" has two meanings: first, arising; second, increasing. That which was originally non-existent and now exists is called "arising. That which already exists and is further cultivated is called "increasing.
Generally speaking, merit is of three types. First, that which is finite and exhaustible, namely the merit cultivated by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). This is because...

Because the mind is partial, there is limitation; because the fruit is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is subject to exhaustion. Second, there is that which is limited yet inexhaustible: this refers to the merit cultivated by those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Because the cause is not universal, it is limited; because the fruit is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is inexhaustible. Third, there is that which is immeasurable and inexhaustible:
this refers to the merit cultivated by Bodhisattvas. Because the causal mind is universal, it is immeasurable; because the fruit is unconditioned, it is inexhaustible.
The merit obtained from believing in this sutra is the third; therefore, it is said to be "immeasurable.
Why is this? It is because, in order to clarify the meaning of "immeasurability," he poses a question to investigate it.
These sentient beings no longer possess the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span.

The meaning of the following answer clarifies that this arises from two factors: first, by realizing the twofold emptiness of persons and phenomena; second, by accomplishing the two practices of taking up and discarding.
Thus, by giving rise to a single thought of faith, one attains immeasurable merit. This explains the realization of the emptiness of persons and the departure from the [notion of] a person.

These are my four attachments. Now, "self" (*ātman*) is a term for sovereignty; "person" (*pudgala*) is a designation for a master; "sentient being" (*sattva*) takes up the continuity of the past as its meaning;
and "life-sustainer" (*jīva*) functions by connecting to the future. These four are identical in being attachments to a person (*pudgalagrāha*);
they are established as four names according to their respective applications. Because one is free from these four attachments, it is said that there is no characteristic of self and so forth.
There is no mark of phenomena, nor is there any mark of non-phenomena.

An alternative version states: "No mark and no absence of mark. This clarifies the realization of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), which is to be free from the four attachments to a self of phenomena (*dharma-ātman*).
Now, "characteristics of phenomena" (dharmalakṣaṇa) refers to the grasping at phenomena. When one is deluded regarding conventional truth, the characteristics of conventional phenomena arise;
these do not transcend the object apprehended and the subject that apprehends. Because the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) is without characteristics, there is no object to be apprehended.

Because the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is non-arising, there is no subject that apprehends. Therefore, it is said that there are "no characteristics of phenomena. As for "not [the absence of] characteristics of phenomena," this is...

The non-existence of dharmic characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*). When delusion regarding ultimate truth arises—such as [the notion that] suchness, from the perspective of conventional truth, cannot be said to have the characteristic of existing dharmas, yet from the perspective of ultimate truth, it should be said to lack the characteristic of dharmas—now it is clarified that because it depends on the existence of the conventional, it is called "ultimately non-existent.
Since existence is already sublated, non-existence is also dispelled; therefore, it is said that there is no characteristic of non-dharmas either. As for "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*):
This is the grasping at both existence and non-existence. It arises from delusion regarding the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*).

First, in refuting conventional existence, one says it is "not existent"; this "non-existence" appears to be non-existence. Subsequently, in refuting ultimate non-existence, one says it is "not non-existent"; this "non-non-existence" appears to be existence.
If that were so, True Suchness (tathatā) would both possess characteristics and lack them. Now, to clarify the essence of True Suchness:

because it differs from the existence of sense organs and their objects, it cannot be established as having characteristics; because it differs from the non-existence of a rabbit’s horns, it cannot be established as lacking characteristics.
Therefore, it is said to be "without characteristics" (animitta). To be "without characteristics" means to be free from the grasping of both existence and non-existence.

If delusion arises from verbal expression and suchness is neither characterized by existence nor non-existence, then it must be that the sphere of mental activity ceases and the path of language is cut off.
If this is so, what does the Tathāgata speak? Now it is clarified that although true suchness is inexpressible, [it is nevertheless taught].
Due to the Buddha’s skillful means, he may speak of it as having marks or as being markless; therefore, it is said that there is no "marklessness. In summary:
because True Suchness is not existent, the extreme of superimposition is extinguished; because it is not non-existent, the extreme of denial is extinguished;

because it is neither existent nor non-existent, the extreme of contradiction is extinguished; and because it is neither non-existent nor non-non-existent, the extreme of conceptual proliferation is extinguished.
Why is this? It is because he wishes to clarify the meaning of the exhaustion of hindrances that he poses a question to investigate it.
If these sentient beings take up signs with their minds, they will become attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
The meaning of the answer clarifies that the grasping at a self of phenomena (*dharma-ātma-grāha*) is the cause, while the grasping at a self of persons (*pudgala-ātma-grāha*) is the effect.

Since the grasping at a person is severed, it does not arise; since the grasping at phenomena is suppressed, it does not manifest. Therefore, the treatise states: "When there is only ignorance, there are no manifest coarse afflictions.
If the mind grasps at signs, this is the active state of the grasping at phenomena, which gives rise to attachment to a self and the grasping at a person."
This is the general response given above; below, it is explained in detail.
"If one grasps at the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), one then becomes attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
This clarifies that when there is attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) in the mind, attachment to persons (*pudgalagrāha*) arises once again.
Why is this? If one grasps at the marks of what is not the Dharma, one immediately becomes attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
This clarifies that when there is attachment to the non-existence of dharmas, attachment to persons arises once again.
Therefore, one should not grasp at the Dharma, nor should one grasp at what is non-Dharma.
Next, he concludes by establishing the two modes of grasping and relinquishing: "One should not grasp at the Dharma" means that one should not cling to the words in order to grasp the meaning;
this is to cause the relinquishing of the words. This demonstrates the characteristic of correct hearing. "One should not grasp at what is non-Dharma" means that one should follow the words...
Take the meaning. One must not categorically dismiss the text as being contrary to the Dharma, nor should one insist solely on clinging to the literal words. This is the characteristic of true faith.
For this reason, the Tathāgata has constantly said: "O bhikṣus, understand my teaching of the Dharma to be like the simile of the raft."
Even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone that which is not the Dharma.
This is illustrated by means of a metaphor: a raft is to be taken up for the purpose of crossing over, but once the shore is reached, it must be abandoned. The cultivation of the Path is likewise:
one takes up the "fishing trap" (the words) because they lead to the realization of the principle, but once the principle is attained, one must abandon the trap. To cling to the literal text...

If one abandons even that which is a wholesome mind because it is considered a "dharma," yet clings to the literal text as being non-dharma, this is an unwholesome mind and must certainly be abandoned.
Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
"Does the Tathāgata have any dharma that he teaches?
Next, the following section concerns the severance of doubts regarding the true fruit. The doubt is as follows: it was previously stated that one cannot see the Tathāgata by means of signs.
Thus, the Tathāgata is without marks (*animitta*). Within the state of being without marks, there is neither movement nor action.

Why, then, did the World-Honored One attain enlightenment upon a seat of grass and point to Kauṇḍinya while preaching the Dharma? The Buddha, wishing to sever this doubt, therefore posed this question.
Subhūti said, "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught,
there is no fixed dharma called 'anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,' nor is there any fixed dharma that a Tathāgata can speak of."
The response below clarifies that the Buddha possesses three bodies: the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The Dharma-body has suchness as its essence; the Reward-body has wisdom as its essence; and the Transformation-body has form as its essence. That which is without cognition and without speech is called the Dharma-body;
that which possesses cognition but lacks speech is called the Reward-body; and that which possesses speech but lacks cognition is called the Transformation-body. Subhūti then said:
The Tathāgata certainly takes True Suchness (tathatā) as his essence. Since True Suchness is neither a phenomenon (dharma) nor a non-phenomenon, it is said:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, awakening (bodhi) is that which is attained and that which is taught, while the Tathāgata is the one who attains and the one who teaches.
Awakening is neither a phenomenon nor a non-phenomenon; therefore, there is nothing attained and nothing taught. Thus it is with the Tathāgata.
It is neither dharma nor non-dharma; therefore, there is nothing that can be attained or taught. Thus it is said:
"There is no fixed dharma named bodhi, nor is there any fixed dharma that a Tathāgata can teach."
Why is this? It is because he wishes to realize the intent that is beyond verbal expression; thus, he poses a question to investigate it.
All dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are ungraspable and inexpressible; they are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas.

The meaning of the answer clarifies that although the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) does speak, the meaning it expresses is extremely profound and transcends the sphere of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

Therefore, listeners cannot apprehend it through the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) by grasping it as having the two characteristics of existence or non-existence; hence, it is said to be "unapprehendable.

Furthermore, the principle revealed is subtle and transcends the sphere of the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). Thus, the speaker cannot [express it] through the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*) as having the two [characteristics of] existence or non-existence.

They are described as such; therefore, they are said to be "inexpressible. Because they are free from the nature of existence (*bhāva*), they are not dharmas; because they are free from the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*), they are not non-dharmas.

This is precisely the meaning of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, which states: "The one who preaches the Dharma has nothing to say and nothing to show; the one who listens to the Dharma has nothing to hear and nothing to attain.
If it were the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) that could preach, why would the treatise state that the response-body and the transformation-body are not [the ultimate]?

Is the true Buddha also not a speaker of the Dharma? Since it is said that the transformation Buddha (nirmāṇakāya) is not the true Buddha, it follows that his transformative teaching is not the true teaching.

Furthermore, because it is taught that there is no fixed characteristic, it is said: "It is neither speaking nor non-speaking; the transformation Buddha has the characteristic of indeterminate speaking."
Why is this so? Because all worthy and noble ones (ārya) are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
To reveal that what has been taught is neither dharma nor non-dharma, he cites the realized fruits to clarify it:
among those who realize the unconditioned, the shallowest is named *srotāpanna*, while the deepest is named Buddha. This is its [meaning].

This is the distinction. The one who is capable of awakening is the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) alone. Because the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) awakens in this manner, the *nirmāṇakāya* speaks in this manner.
Since that which is awakened to is neither dharma nor non-dharma, that which is spoken is likewise neither dharma nor non-dharma.
The reason for speaking generally of all worthies and sages is the desire to reveal that all sages equally realize the Unborn (*anutpāda*).
"It is the essence of activity.
Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill the three-thousandfold world system with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would the merit obtained by that person be great?"
From here on, the function of severing doubt is clearly revealed. Generally, one who harbors doubt regarding the sūtras conceives slander and thereby generates demerit;
one who has no doubt regarding the sūtras accepts them with faith and thereby generates merit.
To reveal that although the Dharma taught is neither graspable nor expressible, nevertheless, by receiving the teaching that expresses it, one generates boundless merit; therefore, for this reason...
Question: One Mount Sumeru, one sun and moon, and one set of four continents constitute a small world-system (*sāhasracūḍika-lokadhātu*).

Taking this small world-system as the basis, when its number reaches one thousand, it is called a small thousand-world system (*sāhasralokadhātu*). Taking this small thousand-world system as the basis—
When that number reaches one thousand, it is called a middle chiliocosm. Taking the middle chiliocosm as the base, when its number reaches one thousand, it is called a great trichiliocosm.
In total, there are ten billion Mount Sumerus, ten billion suns and moons, and ten billion sets of four continents.
They are formed simultaneously and destroyed simultaneously. Below, they reach the wind-circle; above, they extend to the peak of existence. One...
The realm presided over by the Buddha is called a trichiliocosm. Now I ask:
if someone were to bestow jewels equal in measure to this, would the merit produced thereby be great?
Subhūti said, “It is very much so, World-Honored One.
Since the measure of these rare treasures is vast, the principle by which merit is generated is even more accumulated; therefore, he says it is ‘very much so.’”
Why is this? Because it was intended to clarify that although this merit is vast, it is not yet superior; therefore, a question was first raised to investigate it:
for what reason is this merit said to be "much"?
"This merit is, in fact, not the nature of merit.

The intent of this response clarifies that there are two kinds of merit: first, that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*); second, that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*). "Merit" (*puṇya*) has two meanings:

first, the sense of accumulation; second, the sense of progression. Accumulation refers to the gathering together of the substance of merit; progression refers to advancing toward enlightenment (*bodhi*). This is merit.
That which is "merit with outflows" is not "merit without outflows.
Because it is merit with outflows, it possesses the sense of accumulation; because it is not merit without outflows, it lacks the sense of progression.
Does that which lacks the sense of progression bear no fruit at all? It does indeed receive retribution with outflows.
Therefore, there is no principle of non-resultant fruit; once retribution is exhausted, it ceases. Thus, there is no sense of further progression.
For this reason, the Tathāgata said that the merit is great.
Subhūti, setting aside his own teacher’s mind, further cites the Tathāgata as a witness:
"If there should be another person who, from this sutra, receives and upholds even as little as a four-line verse and explains it for others."
The merit of that person is superior to the former.
By receiving and upholding even four lines of verse, one receives the gift of Dharma from another; by explaining it for others, one gives the gift of Dharma to them.

By receiving the gift of Dharma from another, the light of wisdom arises from one’s own hearing-wisdom (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*); by giving the gift of Dharma to others, the light of wisdom arises in the hearing-wisdom of others. If a person...

If one can personally abide in the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), one’s merit already surpasses that [of others]; how much more so if one personally abides in both the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) and the wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

If one causes another to abide in the wisdom derived from hearing, one’s merit already surpasses that; how much more so if one causes another to abide in both the wisdom derived from reflection and the wisdom derived from cultivation.
Why is this? Subhūti, all Buddhas and the Dharma of the unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas—all emerge from this sūtra.

Bodhi is the Dharma-body; the Buddhas are the two bodies of the Response and Transformation. "Bodhi" (Awakening) refers to emergence, meaning the manifestation of the nature through the departure from entanglements.
"Buddha" (Awakened One) refers to emergence, meaning the generation [of the world] through the attainment of the essence.
Since this sutra brings forth the three bodies of all Buddhas, it manifests the two excellences of receiving and preaching.
Subhūti, that which is called "Buddha-dharma" is not, in fact, Buddha-dharma.
"Buddha" is a designation for one who has learned; "dharma" is a term for bodhi. Since the essence of bodhi can be awakened to only by a Buddha, it is called "Buddha-dharma.
Because it cannot be awakened to by others, it is said to be "not Buddha-dharma. Thus it is taught.

That which is called "the Buddha-dharma" refers to the Buddha-dharma of the Mahāyāna. That which is "not the Buddha-dharma" refers to the Buddha-dharma of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).
The phrase "not the Buddha-dharma of the two vehicles" reveals the meaning of its uniqueness (asādhāraṇa).

The phrase "it is the Buddha-dharma of the Mahāyāna" reveals the meaning of its supreme excellence. By receiving and expounding this sūtra, one is able to bring forth the unique Buddha-dharma; therefore [it is so called].
This constitutes the profound cause for attaining supreme excellence.
Subhūti, what do you think? Does a srotāpanna (stream-enterer) have the thought, "I have attained the fruit of srotāpanna"?

The preceding section resolved doubts concerning the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata. From here on, the following section resolves doubts concerning the Dharma-body of the disciples. The doubt is as follows:
It was previously stated that all noble ones (āryas) possess distinctions based on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);

yet it was later said that the unconditioned dharma cannot be grasped and cannot be described. This is still difficult to believe. Why? Because we currently observe that there are noble ones of the four fruits.
The grasper is able to take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its own fruit; just as it takes [the object], it can explain it to others.
Why, then, do you say it is "ungraspable and unspeakable"? The Buddha, wishing to sever this doubt, therefore poses this question. This question concerns the first fruit.
It says that when a person who has attained the stage of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) directly realizes the unconditioned, they are able to form this thought: "I have attained..."
"Is it a fruit? Or is it not attained?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? One who has entered the stream is called a *srotāpanna*, yet there is nothing entered into.
He does not enter into form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or phenomena; thus he is named a *srotāpanna*."
*Srotāpanna* is here translated as "entering the stream" (*rulaishu*) and also called "flowing against the stream. There are two kinds of streams: first, the stream of birth and death;

second, the stream of the noble path. This is what is meant by "entering the stream": it clarifies entering the stream of the noble path while having nothing to enter, and it manifests flowing against the stream of birth and death.
Since there is no further conceptual differentiation within contemplation, how could one see a stream of the Path into which one might enter?
Since one does not perceive the flow of the Way as something into which one can enter, how could one perceive the fruit of the Way as something that can be attained?
Since one does not perceive the fruit of the Way as something that can be attained, how could one perceive that which is attainable as something visible?
Subhūti, what do you think? Does a once-returner have the thought, "I have attained the fruit of a once-returner"?
This question concerns the second fruit.
Subhūti said, “No, World-Honored One. Why is this? One who is called a Sakṛdāgāmin is so named because they return once more;
yet in reality, there is no coming or going. This is what is meant by ‘Sakṛdāgāmin.’”
The Sakṛdāgāmin—this is translated as "One Who Returns Once. After this person has realized the fruit, if they pass away among humans, they go to the heavens and then return to the human realm;
if they pass away among the gods, they go to the human realm and then return to the heavens.
Because they attain nirvāṇa after going once and returning once, they are called "One Who Returns Once. Having observed within and not seeing a self, [they realize this].
Who goes and who comes? Therefore, it is said that in reality there is no going or coming.
Subhūti, what do you think? Does an Anāgāmin have the thought: "I have attained the fruit of Anāgāmin"?
This question concerns the third fruit.
Subhūti said, “No, World-Honored One. Why is this? ‘Non-returner’ (anāgāmin) means one who does not come back; yet in reality there is no coming.
For this reason, he is called a non-returner.”
Anāgāmin; this is translated as "Non-returner. After this person has realized the fruit, they are born in the higher realms and are not born in the lower realms;
they go forth but do not return. Hence, they are called "Non-returners. Since one observes within and does not perceive a self, who could it be that does not return?
Therefore, it is said that in reality there is no returning.
Subhūti, what do you think? Does an Arhat have this thought: "I have attained the path of Arhatship"?
This question concerns the fourth fruit.
Subhūti said, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Truly, there is no dharma named 'Arhat.
'Arhat' means 'one who does not arise. After such a person has realized the fruit, they have forever severed the roots of the three poisons."
Having distantly transcended the burdens of the four modes of birth, it is therefore called "non-arising. Since one observes within and finds no self, whom could one say does not arise?
Thus it is said that, in reality, there is no dharma named "Arhat."
World-Honored One, if an Arhat should have this thought, "I have attained the path of Arhatship," he would immediately be attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
When there is thought, the four attachments arise; when there is no thought, the four attachments cease. Once the four attachments have ceased, can there be [any further clinging]?
To negate that which is real and then to reify it—how could those who give rise to the four attachments do so by using the name "non-arising"?
World-Honored One, the Buddha has said that I am foremost among men in attaining the Samādhi of Non-contention; I am the foremost in being detached from this.
The Arhat’s desire for samādhi—here translated as "concentration"—refers to the "samādhi of non-contention" (araṇā-samādhi). This is a concentration that distances one from [conflict].

One who attains this concentration is able to prevent the arising of the contention of afflictions within both others and oneself; therefore, this concentration is called "non-contention. Regarding the samādhi of non-contention...
First: the cessation of the strife of the hindrance of meditative concentration, which is the foremost state of freedom from desire; and the exhaustion of the strife of the hindrance of afflictions.
I do not harbor this thought: "I am an Arhat who has attained freedom from desire."
Subhūti said, "I have personally realized this for myself; I do not give rise to a mind that thinks 'I have attained.
If others were to achieve it, how could they harbor thoughts of grasping at a fruit?
World-Honored One, if I had given rise to such a thought as 'I have attained the path of Arhatship,' the World-Honored One would not have called me Subhūti."
This refers to one who practices the *araṇā* (non-contention) meditation.
*Araṇā* here is translated as "non-contention. Subhūti said: "If I were to have any conceptual thought, this prediction would have no basis."
Because Subhūti has in reality nothing upon which to act, he is called "Subhūti who delights in the practice of araṇā.
In reality, there is nothing to be practiced; the essence of dualistic contention is absent from the mind, yet he is called one who "delights in practice.
The name "araṇā" (non-contention) is merely a designation applied to his person.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think? When the Tathāgata was formerly with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, did he obtain any dharma?
Previously, this was to resolve doubts regarding the *dharmakāya* of the śrāvaka; now, it is to resolve doubts regarding the *dharmakāya* of the bodhisattva. The doubt is as follows: [Bodhi...]
"Sā" is precisely suchness (*tathatā*). Within suchness, there is neither grasping nor speaking.
How then did the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara preach the Dharma for bodhisattvas? For what reason did Śākyamuni Bodhisattva personally receive it from him?
The Buddha wished to sever this doubt, and therefore posed this question: "What do you think? When I formerly entered into meditative contemplation, Dīpaṃkara..."
"Did I have any teaching? Did I attain anything from Dīpaṃkara? Was there nothing taught?
Was there nothing attained?
"World-Honored One, while the Tathāgata was in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he truly attained nothing regarding the Dharma."
The Dharma is bodhi; "attainment" refers to realization. The meaning of the answer clarifies that within the Dharma, the sphere of mental activity ceases;
it is not sought by vitarka and vicāra, the path of language is cut off, and it is beyond the reach of names and signs (*nāma* and *sopāna*).

Because it is beyond the reach of names and signs, this is why the Buddha of the past closed the gates of speech; because it is not sought by vitarka and vicāra, this is why the Buddha of the present has severed [the notion of] realization. However—
To say that Śākyamuni’s realization was ultimate is to know that Dīpaṃkara’s words were silenced.
Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-fields?

Previously, the doubt regarding the attainment of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) was severed; now, the doubt regarding the adornment of the land (*kṣetra-vyūha*) is severed. Attaining the prediction involves looking upward to receive transformation;
adorning the land involves looking downward to benefit sentient beings. The doubt is as follows: "If the body is a body without marks (*animitta*), then the land should be a land without marks.
If the land is without marks, one should not take up the phenomena and images of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) to cultivate the ten thousand practices (*sāhasra-caryā*)."
To adorn such a land—if it were to possess marks—how would that differ from driving dragons and elephants through a rabbit’s path, or pouring the Yangtze and the Yellow River into a cow’s footprint?
The Buddha wished to sever this doubt, and therefore posed this question: "Do you mean that within the true contemplation of a Bodhisattva..."
"Is there adornment? Or is there no adornment?
"No, World-Honored One. Why is this? That which adorns the Buddha-lands is not adornment; it is called 'adornment' only by name."
The answer is that it is clearly non-existent. There are two kinds of adornment: first, phenomenal form; second, reality.

The substance of phenomenal form is the nature of matter (*rūpa-dharmatā*), while its characteristic is the various jewels. The substance of reality is the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), while its characteristic is the myriad virtues.
Phenomenal form takes transformation as its capacity for adornment and conceptual differentiation as its object of adornment; yet, conceptual differentiation is itself without characteristics.
Therefore, there is no substance that is adorned, because transformation is based on non-arising; and there is no substance that performs the adorning. Thus it is said, "it is not adornment.
In reality, consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) is the agent of adornment and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is the object of adornment.
Because consciousness-only is non-erroneous, there is the substance that performs the adorning; because the nature of phenomena is immutable, there is the substance that is adorned. Therefore...
It is said: "This is called adornment. If this is so, how could one take up matters that entail attachment and cultivate the adornment of physical form?
Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this way; they should not...

"One should not dwell on form when generating the mind; one should not dwell on sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena when generating the mind. One should generate the mind by dwelling nowhere.
This exhorts the adoption of the adornment of reality and causes one to abandon the obstacles of formal appearances.
