Subhūti, suppose there were a person whose body were as large as Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains. What do you think? Would that body be...?

Not at all. What preceded was the severing of doubts concerning the *dharmakāya* by means of the Dharma; this question next concerns the severing of doubts concerning the *nirmāṇakāya*. The doubt is as follows:
if the *dharmakāya* is *tathatā* (suchness) and *tathatā* cannot be grasped, then the *nirmāṇakāya* is true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*), and true wisdom likewise cannot be...
It is taken up. If it were something that could be taken up, how could taking it up be a burden to the signless?
If it cannot be taken up, why did he take it up for himself as the Dharma King? The Buddha wished to sever this doubt, and therefore posed this question.

The King of Mountains, Sumeru, is a metaphor for the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Its height is eighty thousand [yojanas], which may be called "great. It surpasses all other mountains, which may be called...
“O King. Subhūti said, “It is exceedingly great, World-Honored One.
The meaning of the response clarifies that the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya) takes true wisdom as its essence and sovereign mastery as its function; its essence pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
It may be called "Great," for its function transcends all sages. It may be called a "King," yet although Mount Sumeru is vast, because it is not mind, it does not claim, "I am the King of Mountains.
Although the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is vast, because it is free from marks (animitta), it does not claim, "I am the Dharma King."
Why is this? The Buddha taught that what is not a body is called the "Great Body.
To further clarify the great meaning of the body: there are two kinds of bodies. First, the body with outflows (*sāsrava-kāya*); second, the body without outflows (*anāsrava-kāya*).
That which is "not a body" is not the body with outflows; that which is the "Great Body" is the body without outflows. Now, as for the body with outflows...
If there is flow, one encounters limitations as soon as one meets with objects; if there is no flow, one touches upon and accords with all things.
That which has limits cannot be all-pervasive, whereas that which can accord must be able to be universal. Because it cannot be pervasive, it loses the name of the "Great Body";
because it must be able to be universal, it attains the true meaning of the "Great Body."
Subhūti, suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
What do you think? Would the sands of all those Ganges Rivers be numerous?

The preceding section has clarified the essence of the sutra; from here on, the primary focus is to clarify its function. Because the function is difficult to point out directly through facts, it is measured and illustrated by means of a metaphor.

Regarding the initial mention of "three thousand" rather than immediately stating "as numerous as the sands of the Ganges," this is because one proceeds from the few to the many, representing a gradual process of transformation and edification.
As for the "Ganges River": "Gangā" is the name of the river's deity, and the river itself is designated by the name of that deity. This is the intent of the question.
He said: "Suppose one first takes the sands of a single Ganges River as a count; then there are as many Ganges Rivers as there are those grains of sand;
and finally, within each of those Ganges Rivers, there are again as many grains of sand as before. Would the total number of these grains of sand not be vast?"
Subhūti said, "Very many, World-Honored One. The Ganges Rivers alone are already countless, let alone their sands.
The rivers constitute the general category, while the sands constitute the particulars; if the rivers themselves are already countless, how much more so the sands?"
Subhūti, I now tell you this in truth: if there were good sons or good daughters who, with the seven treasures,
filled as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers and gave them as a gift, would they gain much merit?
The sands of a single Ganges River constitute the first degree of muchness. Taking each grain of sand to be another Ganges River constitutes the second degree of muchness.
Within all those Ganges Rivers, there are again as many grains of sand as there are rivers; this constitutes the third degree of muchness.

Among all those grains of sand, taking each grain to be a world-system constitutes the fourth degree of muchness. Now I ask: if a person were to give away treasures equal in number to these, would that be so?
“Would the merit produced by this be great?
Subhūti replied, “It would be very much so, World-Honored One.
[The Buddha] answered, “It is indeed great.”

The Buddha told Subhūti: "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, from within this sutra, were to receive, uphold, and even recite as little as a four-line verse for others, the merit resulting from this would surpass the former merit."

Although the jewels given away may be many, the merit produced is small; whereas although the recitation of this sutra may be brief, the merit produced is great—this is where the supreme efficacy of the sutra lies.
Furthermore, Subhūti, wherever this sutra is spoken, even as little as a single four-line verse, you should know that this place is one.
All the world, including devas, humans, and asuras, should offer worship to it as they would to a stupa or shrine of the Buddha.
This section clarifies the superiority of this sutra and the great merit produced by its recitation.
This chapter explains how this sutra can cause things to be honored: wherever this sutra is preached, that very place becomes worthy of honor; whosoever preaches this [sutra]...
It is not that the person who gives this jewel becomes noble simply because of it; nor does the place where this jewel is given become venerable simply because of it;
nor does the person who gives this jewel become noble simply because of it. For this reason, although the recitation of the sutra may be slight, the merit is great;
whereas although the giving of jewels may be abundant, the merit is small.
How much more so for those who are able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite it?
"How much more so" has two meanings: first, to use the insentient to illustrate sentient beings—that is, using the earth to illustrate humans;

second, to use the few to illustrate the many—that is, using a single verse to illustrate receiving it in its entirety. The earth itself possesses no spiritual power, yet even as a mere location, it causes people to revere and look up to it.
Since people possess consciousness, those who uphold [this teaching] must deeply and reverently cultivate it.
Subhūti, you should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, and rare Dharma.
This rare and marvelous Dharma is bodhi. One who accomplishes bodhi is a person of noble worth.
Wherever this sutra resides, there is a Buddha; there, one may honor disciples as well.
Wherever there is a sūtra, there is the Buddha’s teaching; the Buddha’s teaching is not different from the scriptural teaching.

That which is worthy of reverence is the disciple, and the disciple is none other than the bodhisattva. The presence of the Buddha manifests the capacity to speak; the presence of the bodhisattva manifests the capacity to receive.
With these two sages dwelling between them, the place becomes worthy of honor.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what should this sutra be named?
How should we uphold it?
This chapter clarifies that the essence of this sutra is the true outflow [of the Dharma]. Indeed, one who realizes True Suchness (tathatā) attains true Prajñā. From...
True Prajñā flows into Great Samādhi; from Great Samādhi it flows into Great Compassion; from Great Compassion it flows into the Nirmāṇakāya;
and from the Nirmāṇakāya it flows into this sutra. Therefore, this sutra is that which truly flows forth.

Because the sutra is this true flow, though one’s upholding of it may be slight, the merit is vast. Because jewels are not this true flow, though one’s giving of them may be great, the merit is small.
Subhūti, wishing to clarify this meaning, poses two requests. The first request concerns the text in order to seek its title:
"By what name is this text titled? The second request concerns the meaning in order to inquire about its practice: "How should this meaning be cultivated and upheld?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: "This sutra is named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
This answers the first question and reveals the meaning of the outflow from reality (*tattva*). Now, names are used to proclaim reality; reality is the foundation of names.
Those who realize reality can give rise to names, and those who investigate names can reach reality. Since one wishes to reveal that this sutra serves as the realization of truth...
It flows from those who have realized it and returns to elucidate the *prajñā* of those who have verified the Truth; therefore, it is titled the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
"Vajra" takes indestructibility as its meaning, serving as a metaphor for the reality of wisdom (*jñāna*). "Prajñā" takes spiritual illumination as its function, which is the very essence of wisdom.
"Pāramitā" takes reaching the further shore as its goal, manifesting the application of wisdom.
"You should uphold it by this name.
This answers the subsequent question, which means that one should rely upon the names previously established to maintain the meaning of these words.
The reason for this is that the intent behind establishing the names is to cause one to grasp the words by relying on the names, and to seek the meaning by relying on the words.
One practices in reliance upon the meaning; one realizes the truth in reliance upon practice. Therefore, one must uphold this by relying upon these names.
Why is this so? Subhūti, that which the Buddha calls the *prajñāpāramitā* is not, in fact, the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Honey. This further clarifies the previous meaning. Now, that which is called "attaining the truth" refers to attaining true *prajñā*. At the moment of attainment, one discards words and letters;
therefore it is said: "The Buddha’s teaching of *prajñā* is itself not *prajñā*. If one were to grasp at it according to its name...
Abandoning these two views, one upholds this text; such is the meaning of upholding it in accordance with the Dharma.
Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata preached any dharma?
This chapter clarifies that this sutra was spoken in common by all Buddhas. Generally, those who can realize the truth are able to speak the truth;

as those who practice according to the teaching can realize the truth, so too have all Buddhas already realized it and spoken it in common for the sake of enabling others to realize it. Bodhisattvas have not yet realized it, yet they practice together for the sake of their own realization.
This is because it is intended to show that those who practice together must necessarily realize together; thus, it first clarifies their common realization.
Since all [Buddhas] must necessarily teach the same, this question was asked. The intent of the question is as follows:

Is there perhaps a single dharma that only I, Śākyamuni, alone have taught, which has not been taught by other Buddhas? If it were taught by me alone, then my name would be "One Who Has Something to Teach.
If other Buddhas have also taught it, then my name would be "One Who Has Nothing to Teach."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has nothing to speak.
This teaching is identical to that of those Buddhas; thus, it is a teaching of non-teaching. If this is so, then according to each single dharma, all Buddhas teach in the same way.
There is not a single reality that can be collectively relinquished by all people as a dharma that may be grasped."
They preach together; those who practice together will necessarily realize together. Therefore, although what one maintains may be small, the merit is great.
If wealth is not shared but given individually, those who give separately will not realize together. Therefore, although the gifts may be many, the merit is small.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the atoms contained within a great trichiliocosm many?
Subhūti replied, “They are very many, World-Honored One.”

This chapter clarifies that this sutra is the root for extinguishing delusions. Generally speaking, regarding the merit of material giving (*āmiṣadāna*), it gives rise internally to unwholesome delusions and externally brings about the dust of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
However, the goodness of propagating the sutra serves to proximately extinguish the causes of affliction (*kleśa*) and distantly evoke the retribution of Bodhi.
Now, wishing to clarify the source from which the merit of giving arises, it is precisely the merit of the sutra.
...that which is extinguished. Therefore, I ask this question. Now, when minute particles accumulate to form a world-system, the particles are the cause and the world-system is the effect.
When a world-system is shattered to become minute particles, the world-system is the cause and the particles are the effect.
Thus, when a world-system becomes minute particles, these particles emerge from the world-system. What meaning does this analogy demonstrate? It demonstrates that afflictions [emerge] from...
The gift of material wealth gives rise to a multitude of atoms that are exceedingly numerous; these atoms fill all of space. What meaning does this metaphor demonstrate?
It demonstrates that afflictions pervade the entire dharma-realm.
Subhūti, those atoms which the Tathāgata has preached, they are not atoms; they are called "atoms.
That world-system which the Tathāgata has preached, it is not a world-system; it is called a "world-system."
"Dust" (rajas) has the meaning of defiling and coating; "element" (dhātu) has the principle of being a causal nature. Earth-dust is not a defiling dust; it refers to the subtle particles of earth.
A world-system is not a cause of defilement; it is referred to as a "world. This metaphor universally clarifies both meanings.
The first type of grasping (*upādāna*) is not used as an analogy; it reveals that wisdom is not a defiled object (*viṣaya*), and the merit of the sūtras is not a cause of defilement.
The second type of grasping is used as an analogy; it reveals that afflictions (*kleśa*) are defiled objects, and the merit of giving is a cause of defilement.

Thus, the former refutes the coarse for the sake of the subtle, demonstrating that from a small cause a great fruit arises. This is the destruction of existence (*bhava*) to enter into non-existence (*abhāva*), revealing the beginning of birth and its ultimate end.

Extinction. How is this clarified? Now, the dust of phenomenal characteristics (*nimitta*) constitutes the fetters of conceptualization and belongs to the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The dust of afflictions (*kleśa*) constitutes the fetters of heaviness (*dausthulya*) and belongs to the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Although the fetters of phenomenal characteristics cannot be severed by the contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda*), they can be extinguished by the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*). Although the fetters of heaviness cannot be extinguished by the contemplation of signlessness, they can nevertheless...
The contemplation of non-arising severs [defilements]. Although the two objects differ, both are produced by wealth and merit;

yet the two contemplations are distinct, as both are brought about by the power of the sūtras. If this is so, that which is produced by wealth and merit is precisely what is extinguished by the merit of the sūtra.
That which can extinguish is superior, while that which is extinguished is inferior. For this reason, although the jewels bestowed in giving may be many, their merit—
"Few. Although those who propagate the sutra are few, their merit is great.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks?"
This chapter clarifies that the merit of propagating the sutra is the most excellent among all virtues. Generally, causes elicit effects, and effects repay causes;

if the effect is superior, the cause is superior, and if the effect is inferior, the cause is inferior. Desiring to rely upon the two fruits of the Arhat (the *āryasatya*) to distinguish between these two types of causes—superior and inferior—the following question is posed.
The intent of the question is as follows: The Tathāgata takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as his essence.
“The thirty-two marks are illusory phenomena. Can one see the Tathāgata by means of these marks?
“No, World-Honored One. Why is this? What the Tathāgata calls the thirty-two marks are actually non-marks; they are merely named ‘the thirty-two marks.’”
The thirty-two marks are the marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*). The markless is the mark of bodhi.
That is precisely the absence of marks; it is not the mark of bodhi. This is what is called the thirty-two marks, which are the marks of a great man.

This clarifies that the two sets of marks have distinct essences, thereby manifesting the different characteristics of the responsive and the true. Now, the thirty-two marks are of the mundane world...
The superior retribution resulting from this cause is still inferior to the merit of reciting the sutras. The signless (*animitta*) is the wondrous supramundane fruit;

its underlying principle is superior to the virtue of giving. For this reason, although the jewels given may be many, the merit is small, whereas although the propagation of the sutras may be slight, the merit is great.
Subhūti, if there were good sons or good daughters who were to give their lives as offerings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River,
yet another person were to take up even a single four-line verse from this sutra and explain it to others.
The merit thereof is exceedingly great.

Previously, the excellence was clarified by the relinquishment of wealth; here, the excellence is clarified by the relinquishment of the body. The objects of external support (*upabhoga*) are easy to abandon, whereas the primary retribution (*ātmabhāva*) is difficult to cast off.
This transition from the easy to the difficult is also a gradual transformation.
At that time, when Subhūti heard this sutra being preached, he profoundly understood its meaning and intent; he wept with tears of sorrow.
Subhūti, wishing to praise the excellence of the sutra in order to bring about merit, first set forth his own realization to evoke a sense of resonance.
Generally, the sorrowful feelings of ordinary people arise mostly from distress over existence, whereas the compassionate feelings of sages arise mostly from joy. Now, as for Subhūti—
Bodhi-ear hears the sublime teaching; wisdom discerns True Suchness (*tathatā*). First, he takes pity on those who have cast aside their bodies;
second, he rejoices in what is now being taught.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying: "How rare it is, World-Honored One! That the Buddha should preach such a profound sutra as this. Since the distant past..."
"The eye of wisdom that has been attained has never before heard such a sutra as this.
This praises its rarity; "never heard from the past" indicates its rarity in terms of time.
"Not heard by the eye of wisdom" indicates its rarity in terms of practice. Because the sutra is rare, even though the propagation is slight...
However, their merit is great. Their bodies are not rare; therefore, although their giving is much, their merit is small.

World-Honored One, if there should be another person who hears this sutra and, with pure faith, gives rise to the mark of reality, you should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit.
This praises what is unique [to this teaching]. Why? Because this sutra possesses true faith, which is not shared with the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

When the mind of faith is pure, it is faith in the teaching; thus, the reality-mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) arises. This is faith in the principle. However, while the reality-mark can be manifested, it cannot be produced.
To say that "the reality-mark arises" means merely that the faith in the reality-mark arises.
World-Honored One, this true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is in fact no-mark; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name "true mark.
To further clarify the previous meaning: that which is no-mark is not the true mark of the two vehicles; it is spoken of as the "true mark."
It is called the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the Mahāyāna, not the true reality of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). It is that which persons of inferior capacity cannot achieve;
it is the true reality of the Mahāyāna, uniquely attained by persons of superior capacity.
Because the sūtra possesses this uncommon true reality, although the physical gift may be small, the merit is great. Because the body lacks this uncommon true reality, [the merit of] giving...
"Though many in number, their merit is small.
World-Honored One, for me to now hear such a sutra as this and to believe, understand, accept, and uphold it is not difficult.

But if, in a future age, during the final five hundred years, there should be sentient beings who hear this sutra and believe, understand, accept, and uphold it—such persons [will possess great merit]."
This is the most rare and extraordinary thing.
This praises the profundity of generating understanding. Now, faith is the primary principle at the beginning of the human path, while wisdom is the profound art of ultimate realization.
Intending to speak of how difficult it is to generate wisdom, [the Buddha] first extols how difficult it is to give rise to faith. Subhūti said:
That I have now attained understanding by relying on this power is not rare. It is only in the final age that it is truly rare for one to conceive faith through self-reflection.
For what reason?
It is because one wishes to clarify the meaning of rarity that this question is posed to investigate it:
this person has no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no mark of a life-span.
This clarifies that faith arises based on the sutra; it answers by awakening to the emptiness of persons.
Why is this so? The mark of self is precisely no-mark; the marks of person, sentient being, and life-span are precisely no-marks.
This clarifies that faith arises based on the sūtras, which are explained by awakening to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Regarding this clarification of the emptiness of phenomena:
why does it not state that the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) are themselves non-characteristics? Now, there are two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*):
the former clarified the absence of a personal self (*pudgala-nairātmya*), while the present clarifies the absence of a phenomenal self (*dharma-nairātmya*); thus, they are not contradictory.
Why is this? Because being free from all marks is what constitutes the Buddhas.
If these marks were real, then the Buddhas could not be free from them. Since they are now called Buddhas because they are free from marks, we know that marks are themselves non-marks.

The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is, so it is. If there should be anyone who, upon hearing this sutra, is not startled, not terrified, and does not fear, you should know that such a person is exceedingly rare."
"So it is, so it is," thus he recounted their words. "To hear [the teaching] without fear" establishes its meaning. To be momentarily startled is called *jing* (alarm);
for the heart and gallbladder to become timid and weak is called *bu* (fear); to deeply loathe what precedes is called *wei* (dread).

Alarm belongs to the beginner; fear belongs to those of the Two Vehicles; dread belongs to those outside the Way (*tīrthika*). The first person possesses faith in the principle of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Yet there is no fixed state. Because of distraction, the mind is startled. Next, the person has concentration but lacks faith; because of doubt, fear arises.
Finally, the person has neither faith nor concentration; because of slander, dread arises. Because he differs from the first person, hearing the sutra does not startle him.
Because he differs from the second person, contemplating the meaning does not terrify him. Because he differs from the third person, he practices.
He has no fear.
Why is this? Subhūti, that which the Tathāgata calls the foremost pāramitā is not a foremost pāramitā;
it is merely designated as the foremost pāramitā.
This praises the excellence within the teaching. Now, this sutra takes Prajñā as its primary subject;
since Prajñā is the most excellent among the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), it is called "foremost. Because it cannot be measured by ordinary persons, it is said to be "not foremost.
The phrase "not foremost" reveals its unique (asādhāraṇa) meaning, while the phrase "named foremost" reveals its meaning of supreme excellence. Prajñā...
The causal factor is the verbal teaching, and the result is [the realization of] Prajñā. Because Prajñā is supreme, the verbal teaching is foremost;
because the Sūtra is foremost, although the propagation may be slight, the merit is great. Since the physical body is not foremost, although the giving may be abundant, the merit is slight.
Subhūti, the perfection of patience—the Tathāgata says it is not a perfection of patience.
Regarding this, there is further doubt. This doubt arises from abiding [in a conceptual view]. The doubt is as follows:

"If one who abandons the body and subjects the body to suffering obtains inferior merit, then how can one who practices according to the sūtras and likewise gives rise to painful sensations obtain superior merit? In order to sever [this doubt]:

To clarify this doubt, the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) is explained. Why is this? This patience takes the wholesome root of non-delusion as its substance and the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) as its nature.
It is exhausted only by the Buddhas; therefore, it is called a "perfection" (*pāramitā*).

Since it cannot be fully investigated by others, it is said not to be a perfection for them. Having given rise to the supreme patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena through practice based on the sūtras, [one attains this state].
How could it be wearied by painful sensations?

Why is this? Subhūti, when I was formerly dismembered by King Kali, at that time I had no perception of a self, no perception of a person, no perception of a sentient being, and no perception of a life-span.
The preceding section clarified that because suffering exists, one is able to endure it; this section clarifies that because there is endurance, there is no suffering.
Why is this? If there were a distinction between a self and another, one would perceive the difference between the harmer and the harmed.
Since I, at that time, lacked the grasping at two selves, I did not perceive Kali as the harmer nor my own body as the harmed. Since [this was absent]...
Regarding the nature of these two harms, from whom could the sensation of suffering arise?

Why is this? When my limbs were severed joint by joint in the past, if there had been in me any notion of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span, I would have given rise to anger and resentment.
Furthermore, it explains the meaning of the absence of suffering: even when one's limbs are severed joint by joint—an extreme form of harm—one does not give rise to anger or resentment;

this is because the power of forbearance is fierce. Anger and resentment arise from the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*); since that grasping at a self no longer exists, from whom could anger and resentment proceed?
However, hatred (*dveṣa*) is a great delusion (*kleśa*), whereas resentment (*upanāha*) is a minor fetter (*paryavasthāna*). A great delusion may be requited with a murderous intent;
a minor fetter merely deserves to be met with the infliction of pain and suffering.
Subhūti, furthermore, I recall that in the past, for five hundred lifetimes, I was a rishi of forbearance.
During all those lifetimes, there was no perception of a self, no perception of a person, no perception of a sentient being, and no perception of a life-span.
The previous section clarified that because there is patience (*kṣānti*), there is no suffering; this section clarifies that because there is no suffering, there is bliss. Why is this?

By acting as a *rṣi* of forbearance, one manifests the presence of compassion (*maitrī*) and loving-kindness (*karuṇā*). By manifesting the absence of marks such as selfhood (*ātman*), one clarifies the absence of malice and resentment. Because there is no malice or resentment, there is no suffering;
because there is compassion and loving-kindness, there is bliss.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should depart from all marks and resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[The following further prevents such faults: Now, one who perceives suffering and practices asceticism will have a weary mind and fall back into despondency.
When one practices the difficult path while forgetting suffering, the mind becomes light and ascends; this is to prevent the practice from falling back or sinking.
Therefore, it is taught that one should give rise to a mind of non-abiding. Now, bodhi has non-abiding as its essence.
If one can give rise to the mind by forgetting all marks, the mind will immediately merge with non-abiding. Thus, giving rise to the mind by leaving behind marks is itself the non-abiding mind.
This is its essence.

One should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on forms; one should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena. One should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.
This demonstrates the realm of non-abiding. By not dwelling on form and so forth when generating the mind, one causes one to be free from the fruit of retribution.
One should generate a mind that dwells nowhere, causing one to be free from the cause of retribution.
If the mind has a dwelling place, then it is a non-dwelling;
this demonstrates the obstacle of non-dwelling. If the mind has a dwelling place—dwelling upon the two aforementioned objects—then it is a non-dwelling, for it does not dwell in Bodhi.
If such a mind exists, it constitutes an obstacle.
Therefore, the Buddha said that the bodhisattva’s mind should not dwell on form when practicing giving;
this demonstrates the practice of non-abiding. Now, those who ascend to heights must begin from what is near, and those who traverse the deep must begin from what is shallow.
Therefore, those who wish to enter the stage of the non-abiding mind (*apratiṣṭhita-citta*) should cultivate the practice of non-abiding.

The stage of the non-abiding mind begins from the first bhūmi (*prathamā bhūmi*) and above; the stage of the practice of non-abiding extends from the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) down to the stage of the seeds of the path (*mārgajñatā*).

Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The six pāramitās of the stage of aspiration and delight (*adhimukti-caryā*), although they are mundane dharmas, are able to bring forth the supramundane mind. Now...
Regarding "giving," it is also comprised of the three *dānas* [generosities] which encompass the six [perfections].
Subhūti, a bodhisattva, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, should practice giving in this manner.
Previously, doubt was severed by means of abiding; now, doubt is severed by means of non-abiding. The doubt is as follows: "If there is no abiding, for whom does one practice?
If one sees sentient beings as objects for whom [the practice] can be performed, one should be called 'abiding in attachment to sentient beings.

Now it is clarified that, according to conventional truth, one may speak of existence and action; therefore, it says: 'For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, one should practice giving in this manner. If...
The threefold classification of *dāna* causes sentient beings to abandon three kinds of suffering and attain three kinds of happiness.

Through the *dāna* of material goods (*āmiṣa-dāna*), it causes them to abandon the suffering of poverty and attain the happiness of great wealth. Through the *dāna* of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*), it causes them to abandon the suffering of dread and attain the happiness of security.
Through the *dāna* of the Dharma (*dharma-dāna*), it causes them to abandon the suffering of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and attain the happiness of *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore,
the Tathāgata says that all marks are indeed no-marks; he also says that all sentient beings are indeed not sentient beings.
This clarifies that, in terms of the ultimate truth (*tathatā*), one may say there is no abiding. Why?

Because all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) constitute the substance of sentient beings, and the substance of sentient beings is precisely what gives rise to the name "sentient being. Since these marks are not marks, their substance is empty and lacks reality;
since sentient beings are not truly born, their name is empty and merely provisional. When both name and substance are empty, where could there be any abiding?
Subhūti, the Tathāgata is one who speaks the truth, one who speaks reality, one who speaks as it is, one who does not speak deceptively, and one who does not speak otherwise.
Previously, non-abiding was explained in terms of outward transformation; here, non-abiding is explained in terms of one's own practice. A doubt arises: if the Way is thus...
Abiding should not serve as a cause for the fruit. If it were abiding in the fruit, how could it further be called "non-abiding"?

Now it is clarified that although the Path does not abide, it can nonetheless function as a cause; this is what those who have realized the Truth understand, and is not something those outside the Dharma can comprehend.
You should simply place your trust in my words and rely upon the sacred teachings to practice.
To demonstrate that this practice is trustworthy though not yet realized, five phrases are cited to encourage it.

These five phrases clarify four meanings: "True speech" refers to the teaching of true wisdom; "Suchness speech" refers to the teaching of *tathatā* (suchness); "Real speech" refers to the teaching of the principle of the Four Noble Truths;
and "Non-deceptive speech" refers to the teaching of the events of the three periods of time. "Non-different speech" is the single phrase that collectively establishes the preceding four.
"It cannot be turned back.
Subhūti, the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata—this Dharma is neither real nor unreal.
Having previously raised these words to encourage faith, [the Buddha now speaks] because some might fear that by clinging to the words they would lose the Way; it is to prevent this that he now says:
It is countered by this. This dharma refers precisely to the dharma of the Tathāgata’s verbal instruction.

This dharma is that which is pervaded by the Buddha’s analytical eloquence; it is that which is spoken through the Buddha’s verbal eloquence. Because it accords with the Buddha, it is the dharma attained by the Tathāgata.
Now, the Way abides in silence; to cling to words is to lose the Way. Therefore, this dharma has no substantial reality. Nevertheless...
It is said that words can point the way, yet apart from words, the Way is not seen. Therefore, this Dharma is not false;
because words can point the way, the analogy of the finger pointing at the moon arises. Because the place of the Way is beyond words, the metaphor of abandoning the boat is employed.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva dwells with a mind attached to phenomena while practicing giving, it is like a person entering darkness who sees nothing at all.
If a bodhisattva practices giving with a mind that does not dwell on phenomena, it is like a person with eyes who,
when the light of the sun shines upon them, sees all manner of forms.
This chapter addresses and resolves doubts regarding both abiding and non-abiding. The doubt is as follows:

If bodhi is identical to true suchness (*tathatā*), and the essence of true suchness is such that there is no time it does not pervade and no place it does not permeate, then how is it that bodhi can be attained when the mind is in a state of non-abiding, yet cannot be attained when the mind is in a state of abiding? Furthermore, how can it be said that the Sage exists within these states?
Ordinary beings cannot abide therein; it is for the purpose of severing this doubt that this analogy is provided.

Darkness is used to illustrate delusion (*moha*), light to illustrate the Path (*mārga*), and form (*rūpa*) to illustrate the Real (*tattva*). If the mind has an abiding place, there is delusion but no Path.

If the mind has no abiding place, there is the Path but no delusion. Although the Real is not separated from delusion and the Path, as long as that delusion is not extinguished, [one does not realize the Real].
One cannot realize the truth through the Path. It is like how, although form is not separated from light and darkness, the darkness does not cease;
thus, one cannot see form with the eyes. If that were so, then the seer would simply obtain it, while the non-seer would simply not obtain it;
since obtaining and not obtaining depend upon seeing and not seeing, what does this have to do with whether True Suchness (Tathatā) is pervasive or not?
Subhūti, in a future age, if there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who are able to receive,
uphold, read, and recite this sutra—

from the beginning of the first volume to the end— taking the general meaning as the primary guide for understanding the application of the text, and from here until the end, inquiring into its meaning.
The essential meaning is to manifest the practice; this refers to the locus of practice within this sutra. To receive, uphold, read, and recite it constitutes the actual activity of practice.
Thus, the Tathāgata, by means of his Buddha-wisdom, fully knows these persons and fully sees them, and they shall all achieve fulfillment.
Regarding immeasurable and boundless merit:
wishing to demonstrate that the cultivation of blessings becomes increasingly superior, [the text] first speaks of the boundlessness of the merit obtained.
Subhūti, if there were good sons or good daughters who, during the first part of the day, [sacrificed] bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges...

During the middle part of the day, he again gave his body as an offering as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River; during the latter part of the day, he likewise gave his body as an offering as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
In this manner, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, he gave his body as an offering.
In the past, he sacrificed many bodies for a short duration; now, he sacrifices many bodies for a long duration.
To proceed from the short to the long signifies a further advancement in merit.
Furthermore, if there should be another person who hears this sutra and, with faith, does not reject it, their merit shall surpass that of the former; how much more so if they were to copy it!

One should uphold, receive, read, and recite it, and explain it for others without opposition or slander. Within this, there are six stages of practice from shallow to deep: first, writing; second, receiving;
third, upholding; fourth, reading; fifth, reciting; and sixth, explaining. Now, not slandering is the preliminary shallow faith that precedes these practices. Receiving...
This explains the profound cultivation within practice. Even shallow faith and merit have already surpassed the former;
profound cultivation is truly beyond comparison. Subhūti, to speak in brief, this sutra possesses inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit.
The following section praises the utility of spiritual practice to encourage the resolve of practitioners.
This chapter clarifies that the realm is profound, beyond the reach of mind and speech, and thus inconceivable; it cannot be measured by the balance scale and is therefore immeasurable.
The Tathāgata speaks for those who have set out upon the Mahāyāna; he speaks for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle (anuttarayāna).
This chapter clarifies the greatness of the basis (*āśraya-mahattva*), as it carries one beyond the scope of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*);

hence it is called "Mahāyāna. Because it reveals that which lies beyond the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), it is termed "Supreme. According to the Buddha’s teaching, there are three [aspects]: first, the teaching of the Four Noble Truths (*catur-āryasatya*). That is to say:

The Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is the second, the superior teaching, which expounds the six perfections; this is the Mahāyāna. The third is the most superior teaching, which expounds the three natures of non-existence;
this is the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). This sutra is taught for those who have set out upon the latter two vehicles; therefore, it relies upon the Great [Vehicle].
If there are those who can receive, uphold, read, and recite [this sutra], and explain it extensively for others, the Tathāgata knows these people completely and sees these people completely;
they shall all achieve immeasurable, incomparable, boundless, and inconceivable merit.
This chapter elucidates the seeds that fill the realms (*dhātu-bīja*). These "seeds of the realm" are precisely the three kinds of Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*):

first, the Buddha-nature abiding in its own nature (*prakṛti-stha-gotra*); second, the Buddha-nature brought forth (*samudānīta-gotra*); and third, the Buddha-nature of the fruit of ultimate virtue (*phala-guṇa-gotra*).

The Buddha-nature abiding in its own nature is the realm of *tathatā*. The Buddha-nature brought forth is the bodhicitta. The Buddha-nature of the fruit of ultimate virtue consists of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).

Regarding practice: the first term is "element" (*dhātu*) and the latter two are "seeds" (*bīja*). That is to say, based upon the element of true suchness (*tathatā*), the seeds of sprouts are produced;
therefore, they are collectively termed "elements and seeds. If a person initiates practice in reliance upon the sūtras, immeasurable merit will arise.
Because they correspond with these three natures, they are able to fulfill the seeds of the dharmadhātu.
Such persons as these, therefore, shoulder the burden of the Tathāgata’s anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This chapter elucidates the upholding of the True Dharma (*saddharma*). The True Dharma is itself *bodhi*. *Bodhi* means awakening. There are four kinds of awakening:

first, that which is to be awakened to (*bodhya*), namely *tathatā* (suchness), which is the object-condition of awakening; second, perfect awakening (*abhisambodha*), namely true gnosis (*jñāna*), which is the essence of awakening;

third, the factors of awakening (*bodhipakṣa*), namely merit (*puṇya*), which is the cause of awakening; and fourth, that which causes awakening (*bodhana*), namely the correct teaching (*saddharma-deśanā*), which is the awakening itself.
This is its function. If a person practices according to the correct teaching, this is the upholding of awakening;

by relying on the correct teaching, one cultivates correct practice, which is the upholding of the factors of awakening (*bodhipakṣa*). By relying on correct practice, true wisdom arises, which is the upholding of perfect awakening.
By relying on true wisdom, one realizes suchness, which is the upholding of what ought to be awakened to. "Upholding" is precisely what it means to bear the burden.

Why is this? Subhūti, those who delight in inferior dharmas and are attached to the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span will be unable to hear, receive, read, recite, or explain this sūtra for the liberation of others.

This chapter clarifies the difficulty of hearing [this teaching] with faith. Those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle are the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; those attached to a self are the heterodox and ordinary worldlings.
Delighting in the Lesser reveals they lack the capacity to receive the Great; being attached to a self is diametrically opposed to the True Self (anātman).
Since these individuals are not vessels for the Dharma, how could it be that [the teaching] is bestowed upon them in vain?
Subhūti, wherever this sutra may be found, it should be honored by all the world—gods, humans, and asuras.
You should know that such a place is itself a stupa; everyone should pay homage, prostrate, and circumambulate it with reverence.
Various incenses and flowers were scattered upon that place.
This chapter clarifies the formation of the sacred site (*sthāna*). To reverently circumambulate it is the internal site; to scatter flowers and incense there is the external offering.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if good sons or good daughters who uphold, read, and recite this sutra are treated with contempt by others,
their karmic offenses from previous lives— which would otherwise have caused them to fall into the evil realms—
are extinguished by virtue of being so slighted in the present life. They shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

This chapter clarifies the purification of the three obstacles: first, the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); second, the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*); and third, the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*).

By the power of the sūtra, that which is heavy is transformed into light, and that which is long is shortened; this is the meaning of "purification. To be treated with contempt by others is the transformation of the obstacle of retribution.
The extinction of sins from previous lives is the transformation of the obstacle of karma. The attainment of *bodhi* is the extinction of the obstacle of afflictions.
Subhūti, I recall that in the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara,
I encountered eight hundred and forty million nayutas of Buddhas, all of whom I served and made offerings to, none of whom I failed to honor. If, moreover,
there should be someone in the final age who is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit they shall obtain— [will be even greater].
Compared to the merit from my offerings to all the Buddhas, this does not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth, ten-thousandth, or ten-millionth;
it cannot be reached even by calculation or analogy.
This chapter clarifies the swift realization of the fruit. *Asaṃkhyeya* means "incalculable.
In the foreign systems of calculation, there are sixty numerical positions; beyond these, only a Buddha can know them, hence they are called *asaṃkhyeya*.
Now, if the merit of serving the Buddha is taken as one part, the merit of upholding this sutra is a hundred parts. The merit of serving the Buddha is but one part.
It does not equal even one-hundredth part of the merit of the sūtra.

Next, taking that one-hundredth part and dividing it into a thousand parts, it still does not equal even one-thousandth part of the merit. The same applies to all subsequent divisions. Therefore, it is said:
"it is beyond reach even by calculation or analogy."
Subhūti, if good sons or good daughters, in the final age at the end of time, should receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra,
the merit they would thereby obtain— if I were to describe it in its entirety, some who hear it might have their minds become deranged and confused, and they would harbor doubts and fail to believe.

This chapter clarifies the attainment of great retribution. First, it demonstrates the multiplicity of causes. To explain them in full would result in such vastness of text that the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) could not receive it;
and because the meaning is so profound, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) could not sustain it. If the ears cannot receive it, the ear-consciousness becomes disordered;
if the mind cannot sustain it, the mental consciousness becomes deranged. Due to this disorder and this derangement, doubt arises.
To slander [this teaching]. Because of doubt and because of slander, one falls into hell and undergoes calamity. For this reason, the Buddha did not explain it in full.
Subhūti, you should know that the meaning of this sūtra is inconceivable, and its karmic fruit and retribution are likewise inconceivable.
This clarifies the greatness of the fruit. In the near term, it brings about the retribution of the Ten Kings; in the distant term, it evokes the three bodies of all Buddhas.
The power and influence of the retribution of the Ten Kings are far-reaching and inconceivable; the essence and function of the three bodies of all Buddhas are vast and unfathomable.

At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how should a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide? How should they subdue their minds?”
The first cycle above was for establishing the essence of the bodhisattva practice; from here on, the second cycle is for severing the obstacles to the bodhisattva practice.

Why is this? At the beginning of the first cycle, the Bodhisattva was taught to initiate the three practices. Those whose engagement in the practice was profound forgot their own minds and abandoned all attachments.
However, those whose progress was more recent might still retain a sense of capability and grasp at it for themselves, saying, "I am able."
"I abide thus; I am able to cultivate thus; I am able to subdue thus; I am truly a bodhisattva. Now, where there is a self, there is abiding;
where there is abiding, there is obstruction. Where there is no self, there is no abiding; where there is no abiding, there is no obstruction. Abiding and non-abiding are contradictory;
the self and the non-self are diametrically opposed. Such is the mind that clings to a self.
Since one is already deluded regarding the subtle principle of non-self, the attachment to abiding also obstructs the true practice of non-abiding.
Now, practice takes the attainment of the fruit as its merit, while obstruction takes the hindering of the Path as its function. If obstructions are not severed, practice cannot be accomplished;
when obstructions are severed and practice is perfected, the fruit of Bodhi can be ascended to day by day. For this reason, [the following is taught].
Subhūti again requested [the teaching] as a prelude to the preceding chapter, desiring to cause the Tathāgata to sever the profound attachments associated with that path of realization.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Good son, good daughter, those who have set their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
Regarding the "mind of awakening" (*bodhicitta*): one should give rise to this thought: "I should bring all sentient beings to *nirvāṇa*.
Yet, once all sentient beings have been brought to *nirvāṇa*, there is not a single sentient being who has actually attained *nirvāṇa*. Why is this?

If a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a self (*ātman*), the notion of a person (*pudgala*), the notion of a sentient being (*sattva*), or the notion of a life-span (*jīva*), then they are not a bodhisattva. For what reason? Subhūti..."
"Subhūti, there is truly no dharma that gives rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This answer to the initial request immediately severs those obstacles to practice. Why is this? For one who preserves the self cannot forget their contemplation;
one who preserves the other cannot forget the object. For those who wish to extinguish both self and other, nothing is better than the extinction of both object and contemplation.
This is the exhaustion of both [subject and object]. Therefore, the Tathāgata controls the past by having no further objects to measure, thereby exhausting the objective realm;

he leads the present by having no further thoughts to initiate, thereby exhausting contemplation. Because the realm is exhausted, that which is measured is severed; because contemplation is exhausted, the capacity to measure is severed.

When that which is measured is severed, the "other-self" is extinguished; when the capacity to measure is severed, the "self" is extinguished. Once the attachments to these two selves have been extinguished, [liberation is attained].
The burdens that obstruct the Way naturally subside. Judging from this discourse, how could there be a "self" that acts as a bodhisattva or serves as the object for generating the resolve?
Therefore it is said: "Why is this? Truly, there is no dharma whatsoever that generates the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having thus made his request three times, Subhūti [was addressed by] the Tathāgata.
I shall provide but one answer. Why is this? For the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is first; cultivation of practice (*pratipatti*) is second; and subduing [the afflictions] (*vinaya*) is last.
The arousal of the mind manifests the path of inclusion; the cultivation of practice manifests the path of accomplishment; and subduing manifests the path of non-retrogression.
Since there is no initial arousal of the mind, how much less can there be cultivation of practice, and how much less subduing?

Subhūti, what do you think? Did the Tathāgata, while in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, obtain any dharma by which he attained Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi?
[Having attained] *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and having severed the obstacles to practice, one next severs emotional doubt (*vicikitsā*). The doubt is as follows:
"If the Bodhisattva does not exist at this present time, he should also not have existed in the past; if the Bodhisattva existed in the past, he should also exist today. If in the past...

Regarding the statement "it does not exist": if it were the case that Śākyamuni Bodhisattva did not attain the Way by relying on this lamp, then since it must have existed in the past, why can he now, having resolved his mind [on enlightenment], claim alone that it does not exist? The Buddha asked this question in order to sever such doubts.
"No, World-Honored One. As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no dharma by which the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara."
Subhūti profoundly understood the Sage’s intention; therefore, he answered that there was nothing attained.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Subhūti. In truth, there is no dharma by which the Tathāgata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The foregoing has been stated thus, praising those words.
Subhūti, if there were any dharma that the Tathāgata had attained as anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then the Buddha Dīpaṃkara would not have bestowed upon me this prediction:
"In a future age, you shall become a buddha named Śākyamuni."
In reality, there is no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, Dīpaṃkara Buddha bestowed upon me a prediction, saying: "In a future age, you shall become a buddha named Śākyamuni."

Next, the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) is raised to establish this meaning. Now, the essence of "bestowing" (*śāsana*) is to demonstrate the fruit; the meaning of "prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*) is to determine the time.
Since the Perfectly Enlightened One Dīpaṃkara bestowed the prediction upon him for the future, how could Śākyamuni Bodhisattva have attained realization at that former time?
Therefore, the treatise says: "Because the prediction was bestowed at a later time, the practice under Dīpaṃkara was not yet supreme."

"Receiving a prediction at a later time" means that one attains it only after a subsequent period. As for "the practice under Dīpaṃkara was not supreme," this means that through those past practices, one did not yet attain bodhi.
Some interpreters claim there are predictions at three different times; how erroneous such a view is!
Why is this? Because "Tathāgata" is the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena.
An objection is raised: Previously, the example of Dīpaṃkara was cited to show that bodhi cannot be grasped; now, the example of Dīpaṃkara is cited to show that a bodhisattva cannot be found.
If that is so, it is because a bodhisattva attains bodhi that one is called a Tathāgata. If there were no bodhi...
When a Bodhisattva attains enlightenment, they become a Tathāgata; is it not then the case that they are always thus?

Herein we clarify that the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena has "non-differentiation" as its meaning. The suchness of the Tathāgata is likewise. Prior to realization, it is called the "suchness of phenomena" (*dharmatathatā*);
after realization, it is called the "Tathāgata. Although the names are two, the essence is one. The suchness of all phenomena is designated as "phenomena" (*dharma*).
The Tathāgata is like the person who possesses eyes. Since the suchness of dharmas (dharmatathatā) truly exists, the suchness of the person (pudgalatathatā) cannot be non-existent.
Since the suchness of the person is not non-existent, the Tathāgata truly exists.
If someone were to say, "The Tathāgata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," one might doubt this, thinking:
"In the past, because there was no bodhisattva, it could be said that a bodhisattva did not attain bodhi;
but now that there is a Tathāgata, does it mean that the Tathāgata himself realized bodhi? Desiring to sever this attachment, the Buddha sets forth this [teaching].
Furthermore, Subhūti, there is truly no dharma that the Buddha has attained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Previously, you held that a bodhisattva attains bodhi; that was unreal. Now it is said that the Tathāgata attains bodhi.
This, too, is false. Therefore, it is said that there is truly no dharma by which a Buddha attains *bodhi*.
Because previously there was no Bodhisattva, to say that there is one who attains would not be true; because now there is a Tathāgata, to say that there is one who attains should not be false.
As for *bodhi*, its essence is *tathatā* (suchness). *Tathatā* is wondrous existence and wondrous non-existence; it is neither—
The cause is not the fruit; it transcends the realm of mental deliberation and lies beyond the reach of words and images.

It is difficult to seek through vitarka and vicāra, and difficult to attain with body and mind. Yet they claim that the Tathāgata is attained within form and mind, and sought through vitarka and vicāra.
This is not false; who could claim it is? Thus, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
"Awakening (bodhi) cannot be attained by means of the body, nor can it be attained by means of the mind. Quiescence is awakening, for all marks have been extinguished.
Non-contemplation is awakening, for all conditions have been transcended."
Subhūti, regarding the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata:
previously it was clarified that the Tathāgata has nothing to attain. Some might say, therefore, that the Tathāgata never attains bodhi at all;
to sever this slander, it is said here that the Tathāgata does attain bodhi.
Within this, there is neither reality nor falsehood.
A doubt arises: "The previous statement that there is attainment was not real; the present statement that there is attainment is not false. What does this mean?"
Now, this doubt is severed: because nothing can be apprehended within that which possesses characteristics (*sanimitta*), those who speak of "apprehension" therein are not speaking of reality;

because something can be apprehended within that which is without characteristics (*animitta*), those who speak of "apprehension" therein are not speaking falsely. "Not speaking of reality" dispels the slander of existence regarding that which possesses characteristics;
"not speaking falsely" dispels the slander of non-existence regarding that which is without characteristics.
For this reason, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma.
That which governs all dharmas is True Suchness (tathatā), and those who realize True Suchness are the Buddhas.
Since the Buddhas have realized its source, they are likewise able to govern its manifestations. From this perspective, it is clear that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma. This further...
He cites what has been attained to show that it is not in vain.
Subhūti, that which is called "all dharmas" is precisely not all dharmas; therefore it is named "all dharmas."
Suchness (*tathatā*) is the universal essence of all phenomena (*dharmas*). Nevertheless, among these phenomena, there are those that accord with Suchness and those that oppose Suchness.
Those that accord with Suchness are sustained by Suchness; those that oppose Suchness are separated from Suchness. That which is sustained by Suchness exists within the locus of Suchness;
that which is separated from Suchness does not exist within the locus of Suchness. That which exists within the locus of Suchness is called "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*), and it is also called...
Regarding the Buddha-dharma: that which does not exist in the state of reality is called "all dharmas," yet it is not the Buddha-dharma.
To say "it is precisely not all dharmas" is to speak from the perspective of being free from characteristics; to call it "all dharmas" is to establish its meaning based on its identity with reality.
This further demonstrates that it cannot be pointed out and lacks substantiality.
Subhūti, it is as if there were a human body that was tall and large.
This further employs a metaphor to illustrate its essence. "As if a human body" refers to the *dharmakāya*.

When hidden, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*; when manifest, it is named the *dharmakāya*. Because it transcends the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), it is said to be "long"; because it encompasses all phenomena, it is "large."
Therefore, it is called "great.
Subhūti said, "World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata speaks of a person’s body being large, it is a non-body that is called a 'large body.'"
Having realized the Sage’s intent, Subhūti further clarifies the truth by means of the false.

Why is this? There are two kinds of bodies: first, the aggregate body; second, the foundational body. The aggregate body takes the five aggregates as its substance; the foundational body takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its nature.
The five aggregates are divided and limited; True Suchness is perfect and boundless. Being divided and limited...
To differentiate between "that" and "self" is to create duality; to perfect the boundless is to dissolve self and other into oneness.

When "that" and "self" are differentiated, they are called "that" and "self"; when self and other are dissolved, they are no longer self and other. Thus, [in such a state] there is no so-called "great body."
That which is not a collection of body belonging to self or others is called the "Great Body"; it is the very substance upon which True Suchness (Tathatā) relies.
Subhūti, it is the same for a bodhisattva: if they should say, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa," [they do not speak the truth].
Then they would not be called Bodhisattvas. [The opponent] raises a doubt, saying:
"To realize *bodhi* is one's own practice (*sva-caryā*); to deliver sentient beings is the transformation of others (*parārtha*).
If there were no Bodhisattvas in the past, it would mean there was no self-practice; if there are no Bodhisattvas now, who then is there to transform others? The Buddha, wishing to...
To sever this attachment, he sets it forth and brings it out.
Why is this? Subhūti, there is no dharma that is called "bodhisattva. Therefore, the Buddha says that all dharmas [are empty].
There is no self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span possessor.

Because there is no self, there is no one who can deliver. Because there are no sentient beings, there is nothing to be delivered. Because there is no life-span possessor, there is no constant delivering.
If these three are quiescent, this is the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Since persons are already empty, how could there be a bodhisattva within them?
