Therefore, they are called "buddha-fields. If a bodhisattva were to say, "I shall adorn the buddha-fields," he would not be called a bodhisattva. Why? Because there is no dharma whatsoever named "bodhisattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to say, "I shall adorn the buddha-fields," he would not be called a bodhisattva. Why? Because all those buddha-fields are themselves empty of buddha-fields. Therefore, they are called "buddha-fields. If a bodhisattva were to say, "I shall adorn the buddha-fields," he would not be called a bodhisattva. Why? Because there is no dharma whatsoever named "bodhisattva. Moreover, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to say, "I shall adorn the buddha-fields," he would not be called a bodhisattva. Why? Because all those buddha-fields are themselves empty of buddha-fields. Therefore,
The doubt is as follows: "Those who realize *bodhi* merely benefit themselves; those who deliver sentient beings merely transform others.
Only the pure Buddha-lands can simultaneously benefit both self and others. If there were no bodhisattvas, who else would adorn the Buddha-lands?
Who, then, would desire to benefit both self and others? To sever this attachment, the Buddha sets forth [the existence of] these [bodhisattvas].
Why is this? When the Tathāgata speaks of "adorned Buddha-lands," it is not actually adorned; it is merely designated as "adorned.
The previous mention of "adornment" revealed that the land being adorned should not be grasped; the present mention of "adornment" reveals that the person who adorns cannot be apprehended.
That the land being adorned is not to be grasped is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); that the one who adorns cannot be apprehended is the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
This is precisely the emptiness of persons. If both persons and phenomena are empty, how could there be a bodhisattva within that state who would wish to adorn buddha-fields?
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva penetrates the non-existence of self and phenomena, the Tathāgata declares them to be a true bodhisattva.
Those who cling to a self are not bodhisattvas; those who thoroughly penetrate the principle of non-self are true bodhisattvas.
Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye? "Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye.
Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye? "Yes, World-Honored One, [the Tathāgata possesses the divine eye]."
“Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata possesses the divine eye. What do you think, Subhūti? Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye?
“Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye. “What do you think, Subhūti? Does the Tathāgata possess the dharma-eye?
“Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the dharma-eye. “What do you think, Subhūti? Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye?”
"No, it is so, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye.
The preceding section concerned the bodhisattva’s severing of doubt; the following concerns the Tathāgata’s severing of doubt. The doubt is as follows:

previously it was said that the bodhisattva does not perceive a self as the one who delivers, nor sentient beings as those to be delivered, nor the buddha-field as that which is to be purified. Why is this?"
[The Buddha] can purify them. If that is so, does the Tathāgata not see all phenomena?
To sever this doubt, five questions are raised to clarify that the Buddha possesses the true eye capable of seeing, yet he merely realizes that what is perceived is not real.

Now, the fleshly eye (māṃsa-cakṣus) takes the pure sense-faculties among humans as its substance and takes obstructed internal forms as its object. The divine eye (divya-cakṣus) takes the pure [faculties] among the gods...

The faculty (*indriya*) constitutes its essence; it takes external obstructed forms as its object. The wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) has the wisdom of suchness (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) as its essence; it takes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as its object.

The Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*) has the wisdom of conventional measurement (*yathāmātra-jñāna*) as its essence; it takes the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as its object. The Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*) has effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) as its essence;
it takes all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*) as its object. Because the Buddha is born among humans, he possesses [these eyes].

Because the fleshly eye is constantly in samādhi, there is the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Because one has attained the inconceivable wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*), there is the wisdom eye (*prajñācakṣus*).

Because one preaches the Dharma according to the capacities of beings, there is the Dharma eye (*dharmacakṣus*). Because one knows all phenomena through the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇasamprayuktajñāna*), there is the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*).
"Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the grains of sand in the Ganges River called 'sand' by the Buddha?
"Yes, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata calls them sand. "Subhūti, what do you think?
If there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in a single Ganges River, and if there were as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers..."
"Yes, World-Honored One, they would be very many. The Buddha told Subhūti:
"In all those lands, the Tathāgata fully knows the various kinds of minds of all sentient beings."

Having already demonstrated the substance of seeing, we shall next clarify the function of seeing. As for the mind: if one speaks of its nature, it comprises the streams of the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth consciousnesses;

if one speaks of its associated states, it includes the categories of defilement and purity, concentration and distraction. Since these details are numerous and vast, they are summarized here under various general headings.
Now, form serves as the gateway through which the mind is illuminated; thus, those who speak of knowing the mind must also see form.
Why is this? The Tathāgata has taught that all minds are non-minds; it is precisely for this reason they are called "mind.

Previously, it was clarified that through seeing one attains pervasiveness; now, it is clarified that through exhaustion one attains non-perversion. For one who abides in the four foundations of mindfulness, the mind is real by conforming to conditions;
for one who abides amidst the five sensual objects, the mind is empty because it turns away from the objective realm. Being real, one attains the mind.

As for the term "mind": if it were empty, it would lose the meaning of its essence. That "all minds are not mind" reveals that one has departed from the objects of the four foundations of mindfulness;
it clarifies that they are not the true mind. That which is called "mind" is bound and dwells within the dust of the five desires; this clarifies that it is a perverted mind.
Why is that? Subhūti, the past mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended;
the present mind cannot be apprehended.
The preceding section revealed the inversion by examining the objects; this section clarifies their emptiness by examining their nature. Why is this?
Because the past mind has already ceased and is thus unobtainable; the future mind has not yet arisen and is thus unobtainable; and the present mind does not abide and is thus unobtainable.
To have no attainment is itself attainment—this is its falsity. Although all minds are false, the Buddha is their very essence.
One knows it through delusion; therefore, the mind that is able to know is not inverted.
Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would that person, by reason of this cause and condition, acquire much merit?
Previously, doubt was severed by means of wisdom; now, doubt is severed by means of merit. The doubt is as follows:
"If the preceding mind is inverted, is this present mind that cultivates merit inverted or non-inverted? If it is inverted, it should not be called wholesome.

If it is non-inverted, why does it arise based on an inversion? The Buddha, wishing to sever this doubt, clarifies that obtaining little merit is what constitutes an inversion, whereas obtaining merit [in abundance] is not.
"Much" does not constitute an error; therefore, this question was asked.
"It is so, World-Honored One. By these causes and conditions, this person gains exceedingly much merit.
Subhūti has profoundly realized the profound meaning, and thus he answered that it is "exceedingly much."
Subhūti, if merit were substantial, the Tathāgata would not say that one gains much merit.
Because merit is insubstantial, the Tathāgata says that one gains much merit.

Now, while the relinquishing of jewels is no different [in both cases], the application of the mind differs. If the mind of relinquishing departs from true mindfulness, it becomes the cause of birth and death;
therefore, it is an inversion. If the mind of relinquishing abides in true wisdom, it becomes the foundation of the Buddha’s insight;
therefore, it is not an inversion. Being the foundation of the Buddha’s insight, it is ultimately inexhaustible; being the cause of birth and death, it ultimately returns to existence.
[The merit] is exhausted. Because the Buddha wishes to clarify this meaning, he says: "If merit had substantial reality, the Tathāgata would not say it is much.
This clarifies that if there were substantial reality, it would be with outflows (*sāsrava*); being with outflows, it would be subject to exhaustion; being subject to exhaustion, it would be small.

Because merit lacks substantial reality, the Tathāgata says it is much. This clarifies that lacking substantial reality means it is without outflows (*anāsrava*); being without outflows, it is inexhaustible.
"Inexhaustibility is what constitutes 'much. Subhūti, what do you think?
Can a Buddha be seen by means of a body of perfect form? Previously, doubt was severed with reference to the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body);
now, doubt is severed with reference to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body). Merit and wisdom constitute the *saṃbhogakāya*; the marks and signs [constitute the *nirmāṇakāya*].
This is a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). A doubt arises: "The Tathāgata previously explained as the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena.
True suchness is not form (*rūpa*), whereas the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) are form. Since the Tathāgata is form, it would be inappropriate for him to be named after true suchness;
yet since the Tathāgata is not [merely] form, he should not possess marks and signs. Desiring to sever this doubt, the Buddha posed this question.
"No, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata should not be seen by means of the physical body.
Subhūti answered "it should not" because he realized that there is a difference between the conventional and the ultimate truth.
Why is this? When the Tathāgata speaks of a "complete body of form," it is not a complete body of form; it is merely designated as a "complete body of form.

This is because the true body is the essence (*tattva-kāya*), while the transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) is its function. Form is itself non-form; one must investigate this through the lens of transformation.
Entering into reality is what is called the form-body (*rūpakāya*). Flowing forth from reality to transform beings, its essence and function rely upon one another and have never been separate.
One must not see the manifested transformation and thereby slander the true essence; nor may one encounter the truth and yet doubt the transformative function.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of his possession of the various marks? No, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata should not be seen by means of his possession of the various marks. Why is this? What the Tathāgata calls the possession of the various marks is itself not a possession;
it is merely designated as the possession of the various marks.”
The eighty minor marks were explained previously; here, the thirty-two major marks are explained. Since the underlying intent is not different, how can there be any room for contradiction?
Now, the Dharma-body abiding in the world beyond is like the moon in the sky; the Form-body abiding in the world is like a reflection in water.
A reflection in water has no substantiality yet is visible; if one traces its fundamental essence, it is none other than the moon in the sky.
In this month, the colors of the world appear as if real yet are without substance; if one seeks their fundamental reality, they are none other than the supramundane Dharmakāya.
Subhūti, do not think that the Tathāgata has had the thought: "I shall preach some dharma."

The previous section resolved doubts concerning the essence of the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*); the present section resolves doubts concerning its function. Physical marks and signs constitute the essence of the transformation-body;

preaching the Dharma constitutes its function. A doubt arises: "If the Tathāgata possesses form, he may have something to respond to and preach; but if the Tathāgata has no form, who is it that preaches?
The Buddha, wishing to sever this attachment, clarifies that the preaching of the Dharma is not separate from the *dharmadhātu*, just as the form-body is not [separate from it].
Because it is apart from the Dharma-body, I say: "Do not say that I have any teaching.
Do not harbor such a thought. Why is this? If anyone says that the Tathāgata has taught any dharma, they are slandering the Buddha.

Because they cannot understand what I have taught, they take that which is non-existent to be existent; this is their failure to understand. To hold fast with the mind and speak thus with the mouth is to slander the Buddha.
Subhūti, the one who preaches the Dharma has no dharma to preach; this is called preaching the Dharma. This clarifies the intent behind the refutation [of dharmas]:
to preach that which is "unpreachable" is to use the conventional to enter the ultimate; this is called preaching the Dharma.
It is to give rise to function from the essence—namely, from the most pure *dharmadhātu* down to its manifestation as the *nirmāṇakāya*. As for the *nirmāṇakāya*:
This sutra was thus transmitted.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, when the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, was it as one who attained nothing?"

Previously, doubts were severed with reference to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body); now, doubts are severed with reference to the *dharmakāya* (dharma body). One might doubt that form and sound belong to the *nirmāṇakāya*, while bodhi belongs to the *dharmakāya*.
Furthermore, one might doubt: "If those who realize the fruit are inferior, there is something superior; if those who realize the fruit are superior, there is nothing superior.
Since it was previously stated that there is truly no dharma by which one attains bodhi, for what reason is the name "unsurpassed" established? Subhūti—
Wishing to sever this doubt, he asks this question.
"It is so, it is so, Subhūti. In my *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended; it is for this reason that it is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Now, all phenomena are fundamentally quiescent; thus, the nature of afflictions is empty. Since afflictions are already empty, what is there to be severed?
Emptiness itself is cessation; why must it be realized separately? This cessation is none other than unsurpassed bodhi. Therefore, a sutra says:
All sentient beings are themselves the mark of quiescence; they do not undergo further extinction.
Furthermore, Subhūti, this dharma is equal, without high or low; it is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
That which cannot be named as "unsurpassed" is so because its essence (*tattva*) is equal. This essence is the *dharmadhātu*.
When immeasurable sentient beings attain Buddhahood, it does not increase; when immeasurable eons pass without them attaining Buddhahood, it does not decrease.
Because it does not increase, it is not high; because it does not decrease, it is not low. Since there is neither high nor low, what further [distinction] could there be?
Does the Dharma not transcend all external appearances and thus merit the name "unsurpassed"?
Because it is without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-span, and because it is further purified through equality.
"Without self and without person" is the meaning of purity; for its intrinsic nature is pure from the very beginning.
Purity. At the time of fruition, it is stainless and pure; this purity is designated as peerless and unsurpassed.
By practicing all wholesome dharmas, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, it is because the Path is without equal. The Path is all wholesome dharmas.
Subhūti, those which are called wholesome dharmas by the Tathāgata are not wholesome dharmas; they are designated as "wholesome dharmas."
"Good" (*kuśala*) is a name for being free from evil; "dharma" has the meaning of that which can maintain. Non-outflowing goodness (*anāsrava-kuśala*) possesses two functions:
first, it is the removal of obstructions; second, it maintains the truth. When speaking of non-virtuous dharmas (*akuśala-dharma*), they are defined by their function as the removal of obstructions.
These are called wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*). Their meaning is established based on maintaining the truth. From this it follows that there is nothing else equal to them.
Since the cause is already without equal, it has never occurred that the fruit could be superior [to it].
Subhūti, if someone were to take all the Sumeru kings of mountains within a trichiliocosm and offer them as a heap of these seven treasures as a gift,
and if another person were to [offer] this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra—
Even if one were to receive, uphold, and explain to others as little as a single four-line verse, the former merit would not equal even a hundredth part of it;
it would not equal a hundred-thousand-million-billionth part, nor could it be reached by any calculation, analogy, or comparison.
Previously, doubt was severed regarding the fruit of the Dharma-body; now, doubt is severed regarding the cause of the Dharma-body. The doubt is as follows:
"If the cause of Bodhi must be wholesome, then the essence of the True Teaching is neutral (*avyākṛta*).
How can the fruit of Bodhi be attained through a neutral cause? To sever this doubt, it is clarified that while your dharma is neutral, my dharma is inherently so.
Excellent. Why is this? Right teaching is itself the arousal of goodness. It originally arises from reality, yet it has not yet returned to manifest that reality;
therefore, a single verse of the Dharma-treasure surpasses immeasurable worldly treasures. Because the Dharma-treasure is superior, even if one possesses only a small amount, the merit is great;
because worldly treasures are inferior, even if one gives much, the merit is small.
Subhūti, what do you think? You should not think that the Tathāgata has this thought: "I shall deliver sentient beings.
Previously, [the Buddha] resolved doubts by means of the cause of the dharmakāya; now, he resolves doubts by means of the activity of the dharmakāya. The dharmakāya, by means of all...
Wholesome dharmas are its cause; to liberate sentient beings is its function. A doubt arises:
"If bodhi is equal and devoid of high or low, how can it be that the Tathāgata is the one who delivers and sentient beings are those to be delivered?
Since the agent and the object are distinct, how can there be equality? Desiring to sever this doubt, the Buddha poses this question: "Do not say of me..."
The Way is naturally accomplished; therefore, it is that by which one is able to cross over. Other paths are obtained through me; therefore, they are what is crossed over.
Subhūti, do not harbor such a thought. Why is this? In truth, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata has delivered.
The Tathāgata does not depart from the dharma-realm; therefore, there is nothing that can be delivered. Sentient beings do not depart from the dharma-realm;
therefore, there is nothing to be delivered.
If there were sentient beings whom the Tathāgata could deliver, the Tathāgata would possess a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Where there is measurement, there is grasping; this is the same for the sage and the ordinary person.
Subhūti, when the Tathāgata speaks of a "self," he does not mean that there is a self, yet ordinary people imagine there is a self.
Where there is no measure, there is no grasping; this is the distinction between the ordinary person and the sage.
Subhūti, that which the Tathāgata calls an "ordinary person" is not, in fact, an ordinary person.
One who does not attain the dharmas of a sage is designated as an "ordinary person. An ordinary person merely clings to a self and to what belongs to a self. An ordinary person [is thus defined].
"Such a thing does not exist for me either, Subhūti.
What do you think? Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks?

From this point onward, he eliminates doubt by relying on the fruit [of the path] through the five eyes; from here on, he eliminates doubt by inferring the cause. The doubt is as follows: [the preceding...]

It is said that the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of his physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*), yet he can indeed be known through them. This is like how the essence of fire cannot be seen by means of smoke, yet it can be known through smoke.
If he could be known through his marks, then he should likewise be perceived through the merit (*puṇya*) [of those who behold him].

To sever this attachment, the Buddha posed a counter-question: "Do you perceive the one who has undergone a transformation distinct from ordinary beings by means of false marks that are identical to those of common people?"
"It is not so, Subhūti.
Subhūti replied, "So it is, so it is. One should view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
Subhūti, wishing to introduce the profound purport of the subsequent objection, provisionally gave a shallow answer based on the preceding question, saying: "It may be."
By means of the coarse characteristics within the delusion, one contemplates the wondrous essence within the truth.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "If one were to contemplate the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks, then a Wheel-Turning Sage King would be the Tathāgata."

If one were to compare the marks with reality, then a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) would be a Buddha. If a Wheel-Turning King is not a Buddha, then by beholding the marks, one does not know the reality.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not [rely] on the thirty..."
Regarding the second point, contemplating the Tathāgata through physical marks:
Subhūti, having thoroughly realized that the Wheel-Turning King was not a Buddha, finally understood that one who perceives only the marks does not know the Truth.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If one sees me by means of form, or seeks me by means of sound, such a person walks upon a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata.
The contemplation of the Buddha by those of the Two Vehicles is established in relation to two objects: first, seeing his physical marks and signs; second, hearing him preach the Dharma.

If he possessed the marks but could not speak, he would be no different from a worldly universal monarch (*cakravartin*). If he could speak but lacked the marks, he would likewise be no different [from an ordinary being].
O Śrāvaka disciples: For one who realizes *tathatā*, there is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
To grasp at forms and sounds is the conceptualizing mind. If one seeks the essence of *tathatā* with a conceptualizing mind, this is already a deviation;
how could such a person see the Buddha? If that is so, the Tathāgata cannot be known through characteristics, and thus Bodhi cannot be attained through merit.
...the feeling has also been severed.

Subhūti, if you should think that the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* because he does not possess the marks of perfection, Subhūti, do not think so. The Tathāgata did not attain it because he possesses the marks of perfection.
One attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Previously, one severed the cause of attachment and thereby inferred the fruit; now, having severed the cause of slander, there is no retribution. A doubt arises:
if the cause of merit does not induce the retribution of *bodhi*, then goodness would be in vain, its effort wasted, and it would be subject to annihilation without result.
[This is] the result. Because the Buddha wishes to sever this attachment, he says, "Do not conceive such a thought.

Subhūti, if you were to conceive such a thought—that those who set out for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* preach the annihilation and extinction of all dharmas—do not conceive such a thought. Why is that? Because those who set out for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*...
"Subhūti," regarding the Dharma, I do not speak of the characteristic of annihilation.
One who speaks of annihilation does not accomplish the arousal of the bodhicitta; one who accomplishes the arousal of the bodhicitta does not speak of annihilation.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to give away in alms the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,

and if there were another person who, knowing that all phenomena are without self, attained the patient acceptance [of the non-arising of dharmas], this latter bodhisattva would surpass the merit obtained by the former bodhisattva.
To manifest the meaning of non-extinction, it is therefore compared through an analogy: where there is a self, there is birth; where there is no self, there is no birth.
If a bodhisattva realizes the principle of selflessness and attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they ascend to the first stage (*bhūmi*).

Now, the merit prior to the stages of the ground already relies upon patience to accord with the voidness of emptiness; the wisdom of the stages of the ground likewise guides that merit to achieve excellence.
Thus, if it is superior, one attains the fruit of stainlessness; if it is inferior, one attains the fruit of tainted retribution.
As for the stainless, although the causes may be few, they are not extinguished; as for the tainted retribution, although the practices may be many, they are subject to exhaustion.
Subhūti, because bodhisattvas do not accept merit, the previous section clarified attainment by way of non-extinction;
this section clarifies relinquishment by way of non-acceptance.
Thus, non-acceptance manifests non-extinction, for that which is accepted will ultimately perish.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, why does a bodhisattva not accept merit?
What is the meaning of ‘not accepting’?
The Buddha said: “Subhūti, regarding the merit performed by a bodhisattva, they should not be greedily attached to it. For this reason, it is said that they do not accept merit.”
Receiving blessings is due to craving; grasping at the reward of blessings is attachment. Not craving the cause and not being attached to the fruit—this is the meaning of non-acceptance.
Subhūti, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata goes, sits, or lies down, that person does not understand me.
What has been explained:
previously, the attachment to annihilation was refuted by way of the denial of the cause; now, the delusion regarding permanence is refuted by way of the denial of the result.

Why is this? Coming manifests birth; going manifests cessation; sitting and lying manifest aging. An objection states: those who dwell in the world experience birth and cessation, whereas those who have departed [from the world] do not.

The entanglements (paryavasthāna) neither go nor come. If the causes of merit do not receive worldly retribution, why is it that the World-Honored One displays traces of going and coming, and exhibits distinct forms of sitting and reclining? These are the majestic demeanors of one dwelling in the world for the sake of sentient beings' enjoyment.
Since these four modes of conduct alternate and change, and the three marks (lakṣaṇa) shift in succession, this is what is called [the Buddha's manifestation].
How constant is this error! The Buddha, wishing to sever this attachment, said: "This person does not understand. Why is this?
The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore, he is named the Tathāgata.
Now, the Tathāgata is the very meaning of True Suchness (tathatā). He is majestic and immovable; he is profound and eternally abiding.
Because he transcends the past limit, he is without birth; because he transcends the future limit, he is without cessation; because he transcends the middle limit, he is without aging.

Since there is no birth, there is no coming; since there is no cessation, there is no going; since there is no aging, there is no change. Thus, having departed from the three marks, he is utterly beyond them.
Regarding the four modes of deportment, they are not even objects of the mind's deliberation, let alone the ears or eyes; how then could they engage with sentient beings or be utilized?
This is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). To grasp this transformation as permanent—who could be more deluded than that?
Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to grind the trichiliocosm into a mass of fine dust, what do you think?
Would that mass of fine dust be great? "It would be very great, World-Honored One."
Because it was previously explained that they are separated by characteristics, the True Body (dharmakāya) neither comes nor goes.

Now, because it is revealed that obscurations are exhausted, the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) is neither one nor different; therefore, this question is asked. As for the world being reduced to atoms:

these atoms emerge from the world. What meaning does this analogy demonstrate? It demonstrates that the Transformation Body arises from the Dharma Body. That the multitude of atoms is extremely vast—this is...
"Fine dust pervades empty space. What meaning does this metaphor demonstrate? It demonstrates that the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) fills the *dharmadhātu*.

Why is this? The preceding [section] was the breaking down of the coarse into the subtle; what follows further pushes from existence into non-existence. This is because one wishes to reveal that multiplicity is not real; therefore, first...
He posed a question to test him:
"If these multitudes of atoms were truly existent, the Buddha would not have called them 'multitudes of atoms. Generally speaking, as for the substance of atoms, there are coarse ones;
the coarse reaches its limit at the world-system, while the fine reaches its limit at the *paramāṇu* (the infinitesimal). When they form [a composite], they are accumulated from these *paramāṇus*."
One concludes the world through emptiness; when it is destroyed, one breaks the world down to its ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*). To speak of "atoms" (*rajas*) is to manifest these *paramāṇus*.
To speak of "atoms" as being "multitudinous" clarifies that they do not abide in isolation. Now, if an atom were substantial, it would not be multitudinous;
if atoms are multitudinous, they are not substantial. What is substantial cannot be broken; what is provisional can be reduced until no atom remains. As for these atoms—
Because space is exhausted, it is pure; because the obstacles of delusion are exhausted, the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is pure.
Because space is pure, although it fills every atom (paramāṇu), it is difficult to perceive; one cannot say that what occupies one place is different from what occupies another.

Because the dharma-realm is pure, although transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) are omnipresent, they are difficult to know; one cannot say that what occupies one place is different from what occupies another.
Why is this so? The Buddha taught that the multitude of atoms is not a multitude of atoms; it is merely designated as a "multitude of atoms.
This further proves that the atoms are provisional. The Vaiśeṣikas claim that the infinitesimal atom (*paramāṇu*) is real and eternal, and possesses no spatial dimensions.
The Vaibhāṣikas claim that the infinitesimal atom is real but impermanent, and likewise possesses no spatial dimensions. Although this [latter view] is eternal...
Although they are impermanent and distinct, their loss is no different. Why? Suppose seven neighbors were gathered together at one time.
If this were real, would they touch by a single part or by their entirety?

If they touched by a single part, then the central neighbor would have six directional parts facing outward toward the other six. If they touched by their entirety, then the six outer neighbors would occupy the same space facing inward.

To constitute a single entity, it must be divided into six directions; thus, it is provisional and not real. Since they share the same single entity, one cannot accumulate small parts to form a height.
Applying this reasoning, even the "neighboring atom" (*paramāṇu*) is provisional.
Therefore, it is said that while a multitude of atoms is not truly a multitude of atoms, yet is called a multitude of atoms, it is merely a conventional designation.
World-Honored One, that which the Tathāgata calls the "trichiliocosm" is not a world; it is merely designated as a "world.
For apart from the multitude of atoms that constitute it, there is no substantial essence to the realm itself.
Since the atoms are not real, the world is likewise provisional.
Why is this? If a world were real, it would be a composite entity.
That which is real is a composite entity; that which is not a composite entity is not real.
The Tathāgata has said: "A composite entity is not a composite entity; it is called a 'composite entity' [only as a designation]."
"Union" has the meaning of contact. If union were contact through the entirety of parts, then the dimensions of the world would be equal to those of the infinitesimal atoms (*paramāṇu*).
If union were contact through only a single part, then the world would ultimately have no distinct substance. Therefore, even "a single union" is not truly a single union.
That which is called a "unified whole" is also merely a conventional designation, Subhūti. A unified whole is inexpressible.
To say that a unified whole definitely exists or definitely does not exist, or that it is substantial or a collection, is something known by realized wisdom.
It is not something that can be explained through words.
However, ordinary people are greedily attached to its phenomena.
That which is wordless is what is known by noble wisdom; that which is expressed in words is the deluded grasping of ordinary sentiment.
Subhūti, if someone were to say that the Buddha taught the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span, what do you think, Subhūti?
Would such a person understand the meaning of what I have taught?
The relationship between a minute particle and the world constitutes a "binding of characteristics. The relationship between the view of a person and the view of dharmas constitutes a "heavy binding.
The former clarifies the breaking of the binding of characteristics; this [section] clarifies the breaking of the heavy binding. Now, the person and the dharma are the objects (*viṣaya*);

the view of a person and the view of dharmas are the mind (*citta*). Objects have the nature of conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as their essence; the mind has the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as its essence.
The imagined nature (*parikalpita*) is non-existent; the dependent nature (*paratantra*) is empty. That which is non-existent is not severed; that which is empty can be extinguished.
Desiring to clarify the meaning of "capable of being extinguished," this question is posed.
“World-Honored One, this person does not understand the meaning spoken by the Tathāgata.
When the Tathāgata speaks of ‘emptiness,’ the person grasps it as being real; this is a lack of understanding.
Why is this? World-Honored One, what you call the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span are themselves not views of a self.”

The view of a person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*), the view of a sentient being (*sattva-dṛṣṭi*), and the view of a life-span (*jīva-dṛṣṭi*)—these are called the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span.

This is because they do not understand the underlying meaning. Why is this? If the object of the "self" were existent, then a view arising in dependence upon that self would indeed be the "view of a self.
However, if the object of the "self" were non-existent, then a view arising in dependence upon that [non-existent] self would not be the "view of a self. Now...
If objects exist, the mind is real; if objects do not exist, the mind is empty. What is real cannot be severed; what is empty can be extinguished.
Subhūti, those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should, regarding all phenomena, [practice as follows...]
Knowing thus, seeing thus, and resolving with faith thus, one does not give rise to the notion of dharmas.

The preceding section clarified the elimination of the view of a person; this section clarifies the elimination of the view of dharmas. Such knowledge, vision, and resolution constitute the path of remedy.
Knowing is mundane wisdom (*loka-jñāna*); seeing is true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*). Faith-understanding (*adhimukti*) pertains to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Knowing occurs at the stage of application (*prayoga*), where one compares [the object] but has not yet realized it; therefore, it is called "knowing. Seeing occurs at the stage of correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), where one realizes [the object] and does not merely compare it;

therefore, it is called "seeing. Concentration applies to both stages: because it is the basis for mundane wisdom, it is called "faith" (*śraddhā*); because it is the basis for true wisdom, it is called "understanding" (*adhimukti*). (3)
If one practices in this way, the two obstacles are severed.
Subhūti, as for what is called the "characteristic of dharmas," the Tathāgata says that it is not a characteristic of dharmas; it is merely designated as the "characteristic of dharmas."
"Characteristics (lakṣaṇa) are like conceptualizations (saṃjñā). Now, dharmas differ from persons, whereas conceptualization is identical to views.

Since dharmas are of the same nature as the self yet are non-existent, and conceptualization is likewise identical to views yet is a delusion, that which is real cannot be severed, while that which is delusory can be extinguished."
Subhūti, if someone were to take seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds and offer them as a gift,
and if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon the bodhicitta and takes up this sutra—
even so much as a four-line verse— and upholds, recites, and reads it, and explains it for others, their merit would surpass that of the former.

The preceding section clarified that when the path is cultivated, obstacles are severed; this present section clarifies that when obstacles are severed, benefits are realized. Therefore, the treatise says:
"He manifests mundane knowledge, ultimate knowledge (*paramārtha-jñāna*), and the samādhi upon which they rely, thereby attaining remoteness from those obstacles.

For this reason, he again speaks of the analogy of supreme merit. Although the emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of all Buddhas preach the Dharma, it is immeasurable, inexhaustible, and untainted (*anāsrava*)."
Regarding merit: this clarifies that the gift of Dharma is immeasurable, inexhaustible, and untainted (anāsrava), and is therefore superior.
The gift of material wealth, however, is limited, exhaustible, and tainted (sāsrava), and is therefore inferior.
How does one expound it for others?

Furthermore, ask about the characteristics of the transformed teaching: when a transformation Buddha preaches the Dharma, does he preach by manifesting the transformation, or does he preach without manifesting the transformation?
If he manifests it, the listeners will recognize it as a transformation and give rise to slander; if he does not manifest it, the recipients will believe it to be real.
To give rise to reverence is beneficial; to slander is detrimental. Reverence leads to benefit, while slander leads to harm. That which brings benefit is correct; that which causes harm is deviant.
Not grasping at marks—this answers the question: if one grasps, one manifests their own characteristics; not grasping means they are not manifested.

Suchness is unmoving. Wisdom is suchness; the object is suchness. Because the object is suchness and wisdom is suchness, it is called "such-suchness" (tathatā). Such-suchness is profoundly still and tranquil;

therefore, it is said to be unmoving. Where there is movement, there is grasping; where there is no movement, there is no grasping. Thus, it is taught through transformation that one should not grasp.
"By virtue of accords with the immovability of suchness"—this further clarifies the aspect of transformation. Now, by means of immovability, one clarifies non-grasping;

by means of non-grasping, one clarifies correct teaching; likewise, by means of correct teaching, one clarifies beneficial teaching; and by means of beneficial teaching, one clarifies the greatness of merit.
Why is this? A doubt arises:
Nirvana is quiescence, while birth-and-death (saṃsāra) is movement. Since the Buddha has realized Nirvana, he may be said to be quiescent;
yet since he still engages in birth-and-death, how can he be unmoving?
"All conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows; they are like dew and like lightning—thus should one contemplate them.
The meaning of the answer clarifies that that which moves while acting is in motion, whereas that which acts without dwelling is not in motion.
To manifest this principle, these verses and similes were spoken. There should be nine similes, yet this verse lacks three parts; both the alternative version and the treatise [confirm this].
These nine correspond to the nine types of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). First, the star represents views; second, the cataract represents characteristics;
third, the lamp represents consciousness; fourth, the illusion represents the vessel-world; fifth, the dewdrop represents the body; sixth, the bubble represents sensation;

seventh, the dream represents the past; eighth, the lightning represents the present; and ninth, the cloud represents the future. Now, although the star serves as a candle in the night, when it encounters the dawn...
They shine yet do not manifest. Although their perceptions may be erroneous, they are certain to be exhausted upon encountering right wisdom;
this is their commonality. The vision of a cataract-afflicted eye sees floating hairs; though they appear to exist, they are not real.
The objects perceived by the mind are likewise merely appearances and are empty; this is their commonality. A lamp’s light depends on oil and a wick to abide, perishing anew with every moment.
The nature of consciousness relies upon self-love to exist, and it is likewise impermanent from moment to moment; this is their commonality.
Though illusions may undergo a thousand transformations, the wise examine them and find them to be unreal. Though a vessel may hold ten thousand images, the observer realizes they are non-existent;
this is their commonality. Though dew may glisten at night, it must surely evaporate when meeting the morning sun. Though the body may pause for a time, it encounters the demon of death.
Yet they must inevitably perish; this is their commonality. Wind strikes water to form bubbles; contact with an object gives rise to sensation (*vedanā*).
Apart from wind and water there are no bubbles; apart from the power of contact there is no sensation;

this is their commonality. Past objects are what realized wisdom knows; that which is traversed in sleep and dreams is likewise recorded by the recollective mind (*smṛti-citta*); this is their commonality.

They are alike. A flash of lightning appears as if it exists for a moment and then vanishes; the phenomena of the present are likewise, appearing only to perish immediately upon attaining their substance—this is their similarity.
Clouds floating in the sky act as the cause for the production of rain, and seeds within consciousness serve as the basis for the elicitation of retribution.
Taking the clouds as an analogy for rain: while the rain is yet to come, it is non-existent.
In terms of the relationship between seeds and their retribution, the retribution exists within the future birth yet does not manifest; this is where they are the same.

Because the Tathāgata has attained these nine contemplations, he is able to traverse the cycle of birth and death without being moved. To be unmoved is the Seal of the Dharma; to be moved is the net of Māra.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Subhūti, along with the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
and all the devas, humans, and asuras in the world, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly filled with joy.
Believing, accepting, and practicing [this teaching],

the two sages engaged in mutual exaltation, and the fourfold assembly received its benefit. Therefore, with hearts full of joy and bodies leaping for gladness, they believed, accepted, and circulated it.
